item.title: GA4 custom dimension (not set) for numeric params – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

GA4 custom dimension (not set) for numeric params

Arrow Knots had a GA4 custom dimension registered for the level and still read (not set) for five weeks. Sending the same level number once more as a string made it readable in all 41 events from the new build.

Our Android puzzle game Arrow Knots had a level custom dimension registered in GA4, yet for more than five weeks after analytics went in on October 8 we couldn't see which level players quit on. The level column in every report read (not set). The registration was fine; the app was sending the level number as a number. Claude Code wrote that analytics code, and the record from that time shows no report ever split by the value.

The build we shipped on November 15 sends the same level number a second time, as a string. In the events it has sent since, the numeric slot is still empty and the string slot has a value every time.

41 events, the numeric level empty in every one

Arrow Knots 1.2.6 puts the level number into its level_up event, sent the first time a campaign level is cleared, twice: once in the original numeric parameter level, once in a new string parameter lv. On November 21 we pulled the counts through the GA4 Data API (the official API for reading report data). Of the 41 level_up events from 1.2.6, all 41 had a value for lv and none had one for level. The numeric stars parameter, which holds the star rating, was empty in all of them too.

What split the two slots is the type the value had going into Firebase. Firebase ships event values in a container called a Bundle, and the app's shared Analytics.log helper puts a Kotlin Int or Long in with the numeric putLong, a Double with putDouble, and everything else with the string putString. In this call, 1.2.6 changed the line like this:

// up to 1.2.5: the level as a number only
log(FirebaseAnalytics.Event.LEVEL_UP, FirebaseAnalytics.Param.LEVEL to level1, "stars" to stars)
// 1.2.6: the same number again as the string lv
log(FirebaseAnalytics.Event.LEVEL_UP, FirebaseAnalytics.Param.LEVEL to level1, "lv" to level1.toString(), "stars" to stars)

level1 is the level number counted from 1, and FirebaseAnalytics.Param.LEVEL is just the string "level". From October 17, when the dimensions were registered, through November 20, numeric level and stars were readable in none of Arrow Knots' 3,319 level_up events. Test phones and emulators were excluded with the filter from GA4 installs: 11 of 19 were test devices.

Our block puzzle, Block Turn, shows the same pattern. Its 972 level_up events also carry a string pid, the board ID (for example R001). pid was readable in 943 of them; numeric level and stars in none. level is a parameter name Firebase defines, but stars is one the app made up, and it was empty too, so what decided it was the type rather than the name.

October 27: looking for the last level before uninstall

We found this while chasing a different question. Of six new Arrow Knots players who came in from ads on October 26, five uninstalled the same day. The next day's check, run by an agent, wrote down the task "collect the last level that uninstalling players reached" and queried GA4. In that query, level was (not set) for the whole history.

The first hypothesis was ten days older. During a deeper GA4 review on October 17 we registered event-scoped custom dimensions (scoped to values attached to a single event): 9 for Arrow Knots, 13 for Block Turn. The note said "data only accumulates from 10-17". Custom dimensions don't backfill, so the expectation was that values would show up from the day of registration. Nobody split a report by that dimension for ten days, and the first query on October 27 showed the expectation was wrong. The bars from October 17 to 26 in the chart are grey as well.

The agent's note on October 27 read: "Both apps' Analytics.log sends Int with putLong, so the numeric parameters appear not to be picked up by these dimensions." The same document had the fix: also send the level as a string, such as lv = "25", register a dimension under that name, and get the operator's approval before shipping. The same (not set) and the same fix are listed in the open items of Puzzle game time limits: 3-star par by simulation.

The dimensions were registered; the type split the values

The GA4 Admin API lists the custom dimensions on the Arrow Knots property (GA4's container for one app's data). Today there are 10, all event-scoped, level and stars among them. The numeric world dimension never showed a value either, while string values on the ad impression event did.

We haven't confirmed why GA4 leaves numeric values out of these dimensions, and we never tried registering the value as a custom metric instead.

The AI's mistakes were the October 8 commit 5396a0c (co-authored by Claude Code), which sent Int values as numbers, and the October 17 assumption that registering would make values appear from that day, which cost ten days of waiting.

The fix kept numeric level, added the string lv on the same event, and registered lv as a dimension. It is one line, and existing level data and milestone events stay as they were. Putting the number in the event name was already in use: tutorial steps fire tut_N_done, each with its own event name, so they need no dimension. That only works when there are few steps. The campaign has hundreds of levels and only four milestone events, which left levels 25 to 50 blank.

The milestone events exist so Google Ads can import conversions by event name, and those names stayed untouched. Removing numeric level, or keeping the name and switching it to a string, were also possible; the record shows we added a new name, lv, instead.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The 1.2.5 release the next day had no lv

On October 28, the day after the fix was written down, Arrow Knots 1.2.5 was submitted to production (commit c1f5811). It changed the big button on the daily puzzle result screen and did not include lv. That day's write-up of the release only said that the numeric (not set) and the rewarded-interstitial events were still open. From October 30 the harness (agent runs that start on a schedule with no one at the keyboard) did only marketing work, such as ad budgets, videos and posting, and changed no app code.

The same October 28 document said nobody could tell why new Block Turn players didn't return the next day, because the last board they played wasn't visible. When we queried on November 21 for this note, Block Turn was sending the board ID pid as a string. pid was readable in 943 level_up events, so the last board a player solved could have been seen through it. "Not visible" had been judged by the numeric level.

The weekly check on November 15 raised it again. It noted all 1,306 level_up events from November 1 to 14, as counted then, read (not set), so there was no telling where between levels 25 and 50 players stopped.

That night the operator said, in effect, "if something is confirmed, ship a new version," and 1.2.6 went out as commit 64e4df1. Pre-release tests (unit, on-device end-to-end, monkey on the release build) all passed. The end-to-end log shows only that the app sends lv from the device. Whether GA4 shows the value could only be checked after release, and that check is the 41 events above.

Split one report before release

  1. Don't ship an instrumented build until a GA4 report split by the new parameter shows values. Use an Explore report or the Data API, not the device log.2. Check the type that goes into the Firebase Bundle. For any value sent with putLong or putDouble that you want to split reports by, also send a putString copy.
  2. Custom dimensions don't fill in data from before registration, so query once the day after you register. Don't wait ten days.
  3. Put the numeric and string versions on the same event, and a single build tells you which one GA4 shows.

A request of this shape (test-device filter omitted), with the property number left as a placeholder. The customEvent: prefix is how the API names a custom dimension.

POST https://analyticsdata.googleapis.com/v1beta/properties/<property>:runReport
{
  "dateRanges": [{"startDate": "2026-11-15", "endDate": "2026-11-20"}],
  "dimensions": [{"name": "customEvent:lv"}, {"name": "appVersion"}],
  "metrics": [{"name": "eventCount"}],
  "dimensionFilter": {"filter": {"fieldName": "eventName",
                                 "stringFilter": {"value": "level_up"}}}
}

Run it again with customEvent:level in place of customEvent:lv to see both slots for the same events and dates. Keeping appVersion in the dimensions shows which build the values start in. Counting test devices too, every version up to 1.2.5 had level as (not set), and all 44 events from 1.2.6 had a value in lv.

Before the level verdict

A string dimension lets you group by level number as a category. Averages or sums of the level would need something else. The level numbers in the 3,278 events sent by builds other than 1.2.6 between October 17 and November 20 (including 1.2.5 events that kept arriving after November 15) will never be readable in GA4.

The sample is small. The 41 events fall on four days between November 15 and 19 (none on the 16th), and the levels in them sit in a few stretches: the first twenty, then a handful past level 100. That is not enough to say anything about drop-off per level.

After November 22, with more than a week of lv from 1.2.6, we look at where between levels 25 and 50 players stop. That is the check the November 15 review scheduled for one week after release.

Block Turn still sends the level number only as numeric level. Since the last board a player solved is already visible through pid, what remains is deciding whether it needs a string copy of the level number or whether pid is enough.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Why does my GA4 custom dimension show (not set)?

In this app it showed (not set) only for parameters the app sent as numbers (putLong). The dimensions were registered with event scope, and string parameters on the same events had values.

Can I send a numeric parameter as a string?

Yes, if you use it as a category to split reports by. Arrow Knots kept numeric level and sent the same value again as string lv, and all 41 events from that build showed it.

As of 2026-11-21. Git history (analytics commit, 1.2.5 and 1.2.6 release commits), daily and weekly check documents, GA4 Data API and Admin API queries (read-only, test devices excluded).

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Claude Code on Windows: CRLF broke four checks – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

Claude Code on Windows: CRLF broke four checks

On a Windows PC running Claude Code, core.autocrlf=true checks text files out with CRLF and breaks checks that count bytes. Which bytes ship decides what to fix.

Same repository, same file: one work tree built fine, the other failed after 35 seconds. The document viewer app's engine file was 11,548 bytes larger on disk, exactly one byte per line.

Our harness runs Claude Code on a Windows PC and checks out a fresh work tree for each repository. Git on Windows wrote the text files in those trees with CRLF line endings. The original work trees had been copied file by file from WSL and were still mostly LF, so the difference stayed hidden. In the month after the move, the same cause broke a check four times, in three different kinds of check, and the right fix was in a different place each time.

The engine file grew by 11,548 bytes and the build failed

At 09:18 on November 4 (KST), the harness's daily run built a debug APK of SugarDoc, our Korean HWP document viewer for Android. The build failed at its asset check, verifyRhwpAssets. That task pins two rhwp engine files (rhwp.js and rhwp_bg.wasm) to the exact bytes of the npm release, pins the fonts, font CSS and license texts to the bytes recorded in an asset list, and compares size and SHA-512 on every build.

The first failure line read rhwp.js: size 444510 != pinned 432962. Within a minute the agent found core.autocrlf=true, Git's setting that rewrites line endings on checkout. fonts.css in the harness tree had CRLF; the same file in the original work tree had LF, and that tree had built the app on October 25.

On November 21 we rebuilt the situation in a throwaway clone. Of the 28 pinned files, 16 text files no longer matched. The 12 that still matched were 11 binaries (10 fonts, 1 wasm) and one license file, the Rust crates notice, whose original already mixes in CRLF, so Git left it alone. The output shows 31 files turned to CRLF, more than 16, because the same folder also holds files outside the pinned list: our own viewer code.

Copied trees kept LF; fresh checkouts got CRLF

The true came from the system config file that Git for Windows installs. git config --show-origin core.autocrlf printed that file; neither the global nor the repository config set the value. With this setting, Git adds one CR per line when it checks out a text file that is stored with LF.

When we moved from WSL to Windows on October 18, we copied the repositories with rsync, which carried the LF bytes over unchanged. The copied tree has 40 files today that are LF in the commit but CRLF on disk, but in a tree that Git on Windows checked out from scratch, most text files are CRLF. The harness keeps a separate work tree per repository: the utility apps' tree appeared on October 25, the site's on the evening of November 1.

The dates differ by tree. The CSS budget broke on the evening of November 1, when the site's harness tree appeared; the asset check broke on November 4, the first SugarDoc build in the utility apps' harness tree that the harness logs show. The October 23 failure happened before any harness tree existed, and the records do not say which tree it ran in, but the three viewer files that test reads (viewer.js, edit.js, protocol.js) are among the copied tree's 40 files that are LF in the commit but CRLF on disk. We did not check file by file when those 40 became CRLF.

The CSS budget failure was a 4-byte margin running out

On the site, the failure shows up first in the 8 p.m. handover log of November 1. The build check raised BUDGET-CSS (site.css at 41,055 bytes against a 40,960-byte budget), and the log put it down to another session's layout commit, to be fixed before publishing.

The 23:13 run measured the committed file first. The blob, Git's stored copy, was 40,595 bytes, inside the budget, and the 460-byte gap to the disk size was the file's line count.

CommitCommitted sizeSize checked out with CRLF40,960-byte budget
6ab2edb, before the layout40,49840,956passes, 4 bytes left
33af6de, layout40,59541,055fails

The checker measured the CSS with os.path.getsize, the bytes on disk. Its HTML budget read pages in Python text mode, which turns CRLF into LF on read, so the same flaw was blocked on that path by accident. GitHub Pages serves the committed files, so the agent made the CSS check strip CRs before counting (eed841d).

About two minutes passed between the error and the commit, and the agent got two things wrong in that time. Its first test file stayed under the budget even with CRLF, so it could not exercise the fix; the agent made it larger before running it. Then, following an owner rule that a test which still passes with the guard removed is fake, it reverted the fix to watch the test fail. Its sed pattern was mis-escaped, nothing changed, and the test said OK. The agent printed the values, redid the revert by line number, and only then saw the failure.

The site's tools now turn CRLF into LF in six places, added separately on four different days between October 18 and November 15.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Regex tests expected \n and nothing else

The third kind is a test that reads source files with a regular expression. On October 23 the utility apps' unit tests ran on Windows for the first time since the move and failed in five ways; one was the web viewer's security-policy test, whose LF pattern did not match a CRLF file. One line fixed it: replace \r\n with \n on read (62488f2).

On November 16 the agent writing these notes hit the same thing while re-running the E2E isolation test of AXFamily, our family-schedule app, on an old commit unpacked with git archive (which writes a commit out as a folder). That test removes one safety guard at a time and expects the checker to catch it. One removal regex expected lines to end in \n only, so on a CRLF copy it removed nothing.

Re-run on November 21: 20 of 21 passed on the CRLF copy, 21 of 21 on the LF copy.

The failure message was "the case did not change the file". Because the test asserts that its substitution actually happened, it failed loudly. The revert check on November 1 had no such assertion, so it printed OK even though nothing had been substituted (the cause there was the sed escaping, not CRLF).

Which bytes ship decides what you fix

An APK packs whatever is on disk at build time. Built from the CRLF tree, the app would have carried an rhwp.js that differs from the npm release, so the asset check failed correctly and the files had to change. The site is the opposite: deployment uses the committed files, so the disk-size check was the thing that was wrong.

Don't switch every byte check to "measure the committed blob". On the APK asset check, that would have passed an APK whose 16 text assets carried CRLF.

In the table, .gitattributes is the repository file that tells Git how to treat each path, and -text marks a path as not text, so Git never rewrites its line endings.

ApproachWhereResultLimit
-text per path in .gitattributesviewer assets (bcb1f2f)fresh clone: all 28 matchonly for vendored files pinned byte for byte; on source you edit, CRLF written by Windows editors gets committed as is
checker strips CRssite CSS budget (eed841d)0 errorswrong where the disk file ships
turn \r\n into \n on readsecurity-policy test (62488f2)125 web tests, 0 failedonly for tests about content
git -c core.autocrlf=false archiveE2E re-run (Nov 16)21 passedcovers that one command
clone with core.autocrlf=falsetried Nov 21 (commit before the fix)all 28 matchset per clone or per PC; nothing stays in the repository
text=auto eol=lftried Nov 21checked-out bytes matchrenormalising changes the Rust crates notice
text eol=lftried Nov 21checked-out bytes matchrenormalising changes 12 files, fonts and wasm included

eol=lf asks Git to write LF line endings on checkout. -text leaves the Rust crates notice alone, but with eol=lf a git add --renormalize (which reapplies the current attributes to files already committed) stages the notice's original CRLF lines without their CRs. The November 4 records show neither eol=lf nor core.autocrlf=false being considered; the last three rows of the table were tried separately on November 21.

Changing attributes did not rewrite files already checked out

On November 4 the agent wrote .gitattributes (one comment, two -text lines) and ran git checkout-index -f to check the files out again. They stayed CRLF and the build failed again. Tried on its own, fonts.css stayed at 6,465 bytes instead of its pinned 6,410, and a temporary clone on November 21 behaved the same.

The agent then stripped every CR from the text files in that folder with sed. git diff --stat showed a file that should not have changed: the Rust crates notice, where sed had removed the 81 CRs that belong to the original. The agent wrote that one file back from its committed bytes, and the build passed at 09:22.

The day's ops log noted that a fresh checkout was not re-tested. On November 21, a tree already checked out with CRLF only matched after the folder was moved away and checked out again.

What to look at in a fresh work tree before trusting a byte check

  1. See which file sets the value.

    git config --show-origin core.autocrlf

  2. Count the files changed on checkout. i/lf w/crlf means LF in the commit, CRLF on disk.

    git ls-files --eol | cut -f1 | sort | uniq -c

  3. Measure one checked file on disk and in the commit.

    wc -c < assets/site.css
git cat-file -s HEAD:assets/site.css

  4. For every check that counts bytes, write down whether the disk file or the committed file ships, and pick the fix from the table above.

  5. After changing .gitattributes, move the affected folder out of the work tree, check it out again, and repeat steps 2 and 3 (Git 2.45.2, checked Nov 21, 2026).

    git checkout-index -a -u

  6. When you remove a guard to watch a test fail, first confirm that the removal actually changed the file.

The asset check in this re-run is the Gradle rule ported to Python; we did not rebuild a fresh clone with Gradle. We did not measure Linux or macOS checkouts. We have not listed the byte-counting checks in the game and spelling apps' harness trees. The utility apps' harness tree existed from October 25, and we only know that the harness logs show no build there before November 4, not why.

As of Nov 21, 2026. Git history (utility-app repository 62488f2 and bcb1f2f; site repository 6ab2edb, 33af6de and eed841d), harness session logs (Nov 1 and Nov 4), the daily ops log written in the Nov 4 run, the desk's drafting memo (Nov 16), output re-run in temporary clones (git 2.45.2.windows.1).

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

  • Three agent designs, three judges: the market judge alone would have picked the one that crashed on every KakaoTalk file
  • Capping Vertex AI test costs: a 2,500 KRW stop line missed a 2,956 KRW bill, so we changed the defaults

item.title: Claude Code data analysis: a 130% payback was 76% – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

Claude Code data analysis: a 130% payback was 76%

A Claude Code data analysis put our ad payback at 130% by dividing a GA4 number by a Google Ads number; with both sides from GA4 it was 76%, after the budget had already gone up.

Citing a calculation that ad spend was coming back as 130% in ad revenue, a Claude Code agent advised raising the daily budget for our Korean spelling app one step, and the operator did so the same evening. Two days later the same agent recalculated and got 76%. The numerator and the denominator had come from two different tools.

Two weeks before that, an ad experiment the agent had proposed ran four days past its verdict date, the day set to decide whether to keep it or switch it off. Both times, the first thing to expose the mistake was a question from the operator. Verdict checks have since moved to a run that starts every morning, and late verdicts still turn up.

A 130% payback behind a budget raise

On the evening of October 15 the operator asked the agent to pick up the Google Ads analysis for the app. Installs had risen since an audience signal, built from spelling-related searches and users of rival spelling apps, was attached to the campaign a week earlier. The agent first filtered GA4 (Google Analytics 4, which counts users inside the app) down to this campaign and produced a table: 12.7 new users a day arriving from ads.

A few minutes later the operator downloaded the Ads check sheet for it, and the agent computed payback from that sheet's cost per install (CPI). It divided the long-run ad revenue of one ad-driven user, measured in GA4 in September, by that CPI and got "about 130%". The only caveat it attached was that revenue from the newly arrived users had not been measured yet, so the figure was an estimate. When the operator asked whether the conclusion was to raise the budget, the agent said yes, by one step only, with the 130% among its reasons. A minute later the operator replied that the budget was going up, and the next day's cost data showed the raise in effect from that day.

For the next two days the agent's reports compared one line against the baseline and put the decision off by another day. On the morning of October 17 the operator pushed hard: was it going to keep doing this half-heartedly? Analyse it properly and come back with a decision to raise or cut. Four minutes later the agent reported that the extra spend had not added a single user who ran a spelling check, and that payback computed on one source was 76%.

The same report said: "The roughly 130% payback I gave on 10-15 was a wrong calculation, and I recommended the raise on that number." The operator decided that afternoon to go back to the old budget, and the change was made that evening.

The numerator came from GA4, the denominator from Ads

Payback here is the ad revenue one user brings in, divided by the ad spend it took to acquire one new user. In the 130% calculation the numerator was revenue GA4 measured by following the group of users who arrived from ads in September (a cohort), and the denominator was spend divided by installs as Google Ads counts them.

For the same week (October 8 to 14), Ads counted 21 installs a day; GA4 counted 12.7 new users who arrived from ads and opened the app. The install counts differ by a factor of 1.65, and the two tools also logged slightly different daily spend, so the GA4 cost per new user comes out about 1.7 times the Ads CPI.

Multiply 76% by 1.7 and you get 130%. Both calculations used the same numerator, so the whole gap sits in the denominator.

The agent's first suspicion was the numerator: was it fair to apply September users' revenue to new users? When the new users were measured two days later, their revenue so far, less than ten days' worth, was close to that of the September users. The denominator had carried no caveat.

Six minutes before the 130%, the same session had already put the GA4 cost per new user in a table, and then did not use it.

That commit put the gap down to how Ads decides which installs to credit to an ad (attribution), for example after a YouTube ad view, and wrote that money calculations use GA4. The same day the agent's memory got a rule: do money math only within one source, and before recommending a raise, have same-source evidence that ad revenue exceeds the spend.

Two weeks earlier, a verdict date four days gone

On the night of September 20 an experiment the agent had proposed in a revenue analysis went live in the AdMob console. It capped the app-open ad (the full-screen ad shown when a user comes back to the app) at one per user per 10 minutes, aiming for fewer "too many ads" complaints and fewer uninstalls.

That night the agent also started WATCH.md, a file listing running experiments and their verdict dates, and the cap's verdict date went in as September 27. The rule: switch it off if revenue fell by more than a set amount, or if the uninstall rate did not move.

September 27 passed. That afternoon another session even added a new experiment row to the same file and committed it, and every session that edited the file before the operator's question on the night of October 1 left the verdict log at the bottom a single empty row.

On the night of October 1 the operator sent an AdMob screenshot: match rate and revenue were both down, analyse it. The agent opened WATCH.md first and straight away wrote, "Three experiments are past their 09-27 verdict date and the verdict log is empty."

App-open impressions had fallen 35% at an unchanged price per impression, and the uninstall rate had not moved, so the rule said switch it off. The operator turned the cap off in the console and sharply blamed the agent for the drop in revenue. The agent agreed it had proposed the experiment, owned the four unjudged days after the verdict date, and wrote, "Relying on people to remember verdict dates failed this time."

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Daily-check records stop on October 11

The frequency cap was a console setting, so it left no trace in code, builds or tests. That is why, on the day WATCH.md was created, the agent's instructions got a line: if you are going to look at ad or subscription numbers, read this file first. That line only fires when someone asks about ad numbers.

The next morning, with the operator's go-ahead, the agent created three scheduled verdict runs and a memory rule. They used the scheduling feature inside the Claude Code session (CronCreate), with the caveat that they "only run while this session stays open".

The scheduled verdicts ran on time, and a daily check added after them found, on its first run, the R8 optimisation release (the first build with the R8 code shrinker's optimisations on) ten days past its verdict date. The earlier verdicts had covered only the three ad experiments due on September 27 and did not mention this one.

The last daily check from that session is dated October 11. The next verdict date then passed, and the agent judged it only when the operator asked it to run the analysis on October 15.

The Google Ads asset-strength verdict (the grade Ads gives ad creatives) came nine days late. The scheduled verdict on October 6 noted it as an experiment another session had set up and moved on; the agent first said on October 15 that the value came only from an Ads script the operator alone could run.

Of the 26 verdict-log rows whose planned date can be traced to a calendar date, 17 were judged after it, four of them by a single day. Of the 22 rows due after the memory rule, 13 were late, 9 of them by more than a day.

Verdicts moved to the morning run, payback to GA4 only

The harness in the table is a personal runner that starts Claude Code at a fixed time each morning and hands it the day's jobs.

ApproachWhenResult
Calendar verdict dates; read the file first when looking at ad numbersSep 20 to 22Does nothing unless someone asks. Four days lost
Memory rule (verdict dates first whenever ads come up)Oct 2Fires only if the session talks about ads
Schedules inside the session (three verdicts, a daily check)Oct 2 to 11Run only while the session is open; daily-check records stop on Oct 11
A morning harness run that also does verdictsFrom Oct 28 (Oct 25 to 27 as a trial run that recorded nothing)Current setup. While it was down on Nov 4 to 6, those days' verdicts were not made and a later roll-up stood in
A source tag on every number ([snapshot], [AdMob API], [GA4])Log entries from Oct 28The same metric written side by side from two sources
Payback with the Ads CPI as denominatorOct 15Dropped. Different source from the numerator
Payback from GA4-attributed new users and GA4 cohort revenueOct 17Adopted. 76%
Budget verdict on the dashboard's 7-day ROAS (ad revenue over ad spend)Oct 31Same line notes it runs higher than this week's payback because it uses revenue from all users the campaign ever brought in; raise kept to the minimum

On October 2 the memory also got a rule that experiments costing revenue default to off on their verdict date.

Checking verdict dates and ratios

  1. When you start an experiment, write for each row a calendar verdict date, the verdict rule, and which way it falls if nobody looks that day. Experiments that cost revenue default to off.

  2. The same day, query the metric the rule depends on once. One November 7 verdict ended unjudged because the metric was never registered in GA4.

  3. Make the first step of a scheduled run "list every row whose verdict date is before today and has no entry in the verdict log". Don't wait for someone to ask.

  4. Run that job outside the session. On Windows, start it from the OS scheduler, as in Schedule Claude Code with Windows Task Scheduler.

  5. If a verdict needs data the agent cannot fetch itself (such as an ad console script's output), ask a person for it before the verdict date.

  6. When producing a ratio, write the source next to the numerator and the denominator ([GA4], [Ads]). If they differ, don't decide on it.

  7. Put the two tools' install counts for the same period side by side and look at the ratio first. Here it was 1.65 (our puzzle game campaign case is in Google Ads for a puzzle game: CPI 30x break-even).

The 76% numerator is September users' revenue

The 76% numerator is the long-run revenue of ad-driven users who arrived in September; for the new users we had less than ten days of revenue as of October 17. The reason Ads and GA4 count differently is the analysis doc's reading of how Ads counts, not something we checked. With 13 to 21 installs a day, depending on the tool, a few days can swing the ratio a lot.

The most recent late one, due November 15, was judged two days later. Finding out how the run checked the list of verdict dates each day means reading its run logs, which we did not open for this note.

As of 2026-11-18. App repository git history (98c2ca2, 511d768, 8c50186, ff7a5aa, b5805b5, e4baf6a, 953d002, 6fd977a, 2d3d2b5 and the WATCH.md verdict log), Claude Code session records (Oct 1 to 17), agent memory (watch-judgement-dates, marketing-decide-not-report). Amounts are left out under the operator's approval terms.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Claude Code scheduled runs: state left behind – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

Claude Code scheduled runs: state left behind

One Claude Code scheduled run exited 0 but left two uncommitted files that blocked the same app's next runs, so the next run now moves leftovers to a rescue branch and carries on.

A Claude Code run on our unattended harness finished with exit code 0, and the same app's next runs then refused to start. The run had ended with two files half edited, and from the next evening a second, harness-wide cause landed on top, so that app did not run for three days. A week later, over about a day, four social posting runs posted nothing, and those runs also exited 0.

Both runs exited cleanly; what stopped the next ones was the state they left behind: the git work tree in the first case, the browser connection in the second.

The subagent was stopped 10 minutes after the commit

On November 3 at 09:05 KST, the morning job (the "daily") for our Korean spelling app started. It runs as claude -p, the print mode that takes one prompt, answers, and exits without a chat window. At 09:11 the agent committed the day's checks as 890de43 and handed the production of two short videos to a subagent running in the background. Its last message, in Korean, said: commit pushed; when the video agent finishes, it would continue with an independent review, the queue, and the Notion report.

The next line in the log was printed by Claude Code itself.

In the version we ran then, if background tasks were still running 10 minutes after the last turn, -p stopped them and exited. The notice also named the environment variable that makes it wait to the end, CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS=0. The run was logged as a normal exit 10 minutes and 7 seconds after the commit. The subagent had been editing the video generator script and a production log CSV, and both files stayed uncommitted in the work tree.

One app stopped 30 hours before the rest

Before each run, the harness checks the work tree in a step called prepare. Uncommitted changes make it refuse with DirtyWorktree and exit 3. The README at the time said these changes are not cleaned up automatically. The spelling app's 14:00 social run on November 3 was the first one refused, and four runs in total failed to start for this reason alone.

From the evening of November 4 a second cause stacked on top: uncommitted edits in the harness's own code stopped every app's jobs for about 38 hours. That stall is covered in Schedule Claude Code with Windows Task Scheduler. The alerts on the mornings of November 5 and 6 said the same thing for all three apps, "exit 3, prepare failed", which reads like one big outage.

The game and utilities apps ran normally until their evening runs on November 4, while the spelling app had been stuck since 14:00 the day before, 30 hours earlier, for a different reason. Committing the harness code would not have freed it; the two files would still have been in its work tree. The harness README at the time said that after a DirtyWorktree exit 3, "that repo's jobs keep stopping the next day too", and that a person has to clean up. The November 4 alert did list only the spelling app as failing, but it gave no reason.

The repository shows the result: one commit on November 3, none on the 4th or 5th, and no videos produced or posted in between.

The next run guessed wrong too

On the morning of November 6, the two leftover changes were committed to a separate branch (004f642), and less than a minute later the harness runner got a setting that waits for subagents to finish (1ac160a). A few minutes after that the scheduler re-ran the spelling app's daily, and it finished normally. The rescue commit came from a chat session, but the records do not say which conversation it was or who reset that day's run state before the re-run.

The restarted run described the gap in its notes: the leftover changes "appear to have been reverted before the 11-06 start; only the q005 and q006 mp4 files remain". In fact they had been moved to a branch, not reverted, and the work tree had gone back to the original commit. The run's own commit, e795981, sits on top of the November 3 commit, not the rescue commit. All the November 6 run could see was the work tree and the app's own notes, and nothing in them mentioned the rescue branch.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Four social runs saw only a different browser

The second incident began on the evening of November 11. Social runs post to TikTok, Instagram and YouTube by driving a dedicated harness Chrome through the Claude in Chrome extension. That evening's first run posted normally, but from the next run until the following evening, four social runs across the three apps reported "only Browser 1 was connected" and posted nothing. In the connected Chrome, TikTok showed a login screen. It was not the harness browser.

The rule at the time said to look for the harness browser's device ID (the unique value the connection list shows for each browser) and, if it was missing, to skip rather than pick another. The social runs followed it and left Browser 1 alone. But the rule only covered the error the tool raises when several browsers are connected and none is selected; with exactly one browser connected, the tool went straight to it without asking (harness record). On the night of November 12 an indexing job took that path and opened Search Console in a Chrome signed in to a different account. The rule and the reports called the harness browser "Browser 2", but that label follows connection order, and the morning after reconnection the harness Chrome was "Browser 1".

The rule changed that night (e9fc042). Before the first Chrome step a job lists the connected browsers, looks only at the device ID, and calls no Chrome tool at all if that ID is missing. A run a few minutes before the change noted that the harness browser was connected again. Nobody recorded who reconnected it or how.

The game and utilities runs wrote each failed channel into their posting queue table, for example "2026-11-12 20 Instagram failed: Chrome not connected", and committed it. The next runs filled those cells first: utilities posted its two missing channels on November 13, and the game had posted all three planned channels by November 14. The spelling app's run did not touch its queue and made no commit, so the next day's daily noted "no posting record or commit for the 11-12 14:00 social run" and held off judging.

Keep leftovers on a rescue branch; pick the browser by device ID only

ApproachWhat happensDecision
Subagents run in the foreground and the run exits after committing (the daily's own note)Works only if the agent obeysNot added to the harness's shared prompts
CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS=0 (Nov 6)Waits for subagents; the job timeout is the ceiling (5,400 s for a daily)Adopted
Stop on a dirty tree and let a person clean up (old README)The alert gave no reason; three days lostDropped
Delete leftover changes and continueThe subagent's generator edits would be goneNot used
Commit leftovers to a rescue branch, reset to the base commit, continue (Nov 7)Only one job runs on a given work tree at a time, so leftovers are treated as a dead earlier run'sAdopted
Pick by device ID only when the "several browsers connected" error appears (Nov 8)With one browser connected there is no error and the tool goes to it (on Nov 12 it opened Search Console in another account's Chrome)Dropped
Call the harness browser "Browser 2" in the rule and reports (Nov 8)Labels follow connection order; after reconnection the harness browser was Browser 1Dropped (display names ignored)
Check the list before the first Chrome step and call no Chrome tool without the device ID (Nov 12); log a failure per channel in the queue (Nov 11)The next run fills empty channels firstAdopted

If a scheduled run uses subagents, do not rely on a prompt rule alone. Force the wait in the runner's settings and the cleanup in the next run's prepare step.

Checks for the end and start of a run

The harness now moves a leftover work tree to a rescue branch in the next run's prepare step, checks the browser before the first Chrome step, and writes unfinished work where the next run reads it. The steps below add an end-of-run check on top (step 2 is not in this harness yet):

  1. Set CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS=0 in the runner's environment and give every job a timeout. A Background tasks still running line in the log means the run left work unfinished.

  2. Count a run as complete only when git status --porcelain is empty and nothing is left unpushed. Otherwise record the leftover file list as the failure reason.

  3. In the next run's prepare step, do not delete a dirty tree. Commit it to a branch such as harness-rescue/<time>-<job>, reset to the base commit, then continue, and put the file list and branch name in the alert.

  4. For jobs that need a browser, call the Claude in Chrome tool list_connected_browsers before the first Chrome step and pick with select_browser only when the expected device ID is there. If it is not, call no Chrome tool. Ignore display names.

  5. Write unfinished work where the next run reads it, as "date hour channel failed: reason", and commit it. The next run starts from those cells.

If you call claude -p straight from Task Scheduler without a harness, steps 1 to 3 fit around the call like this. We ran the rescue and completion parts in a scratch repository on November 21 with PowerShell 5.1: two leftover files moved to the rescue branch and left the tree clean, and an edited file or an unpushed commit made the script exit 4.

$env:CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS = '0'
# Before the run: move leftovers to a rescue branch instead of deleting them
if (git status --porcelain) {
  $b = "harness-rescue/$(Get-Date -Format yyyyMMdd-HHmm)-daily"
  git switch -q --create $b
  git add -A
  git commit -q -m "rescue: leftovers from the previous run"
  git switch -q -
}
claude -p "..."
# After the run: done only if the tree is clean and nothing is unpushed
if ((git status --porcelain) -or (git log '@{u}..' --oneline)) { exit 4 }

git add -A also picks up new untracked files, so put large generated output such as videos in .gitignore first. On a branch with no upstream the last line's unpushed check is skipped, so link it with git push -u first. Writing a verdict line at the end of each report is covered in 17 days of a Claude Code harness: how to start.

A dropped browser still needs a person to reconnect it

Waiting for subagents makes runs longer, and a run that hits its timeout is killed by the runner, which can leave the same kind of leftovers. The next prepare step moves them to a rescue branch; if that fails (a commit hook, say), the job stops as before. Rescue branches pile up and a person has to delete them.

Automatic rescue assumes leftovers belong to a dead earlier run. If a person edits in the same work tree the scheduled jobs use, those edits get moved to a rescue branch too, so keep a separate work tree for operations. This harness runs from its own copies, apart from the trees people edit in.

The device ID check stops a job from using the wrong browser; it does not reconnect the right one. On November 12 several alerts asked a person to check the Chrome extension connection, and the browser came back only that night. Runs still exit 0, too: the daily status boards for November 11 and 12 reported "0 failed or missed" and counted these runs as partial failures. Next to check: why the connection dropped, and whether the 10-minute default wait is the same in later Claude Code versions.

As of 2026-11-20. Harness run logs and alert log (Nov 1 to 16, 2026), git history of the spelling, game and utilities app repos, harness repository commits and README. Rescue and completion script re-run in a scratch repository on 2026-11-21.

item.title: Claude Code tapped a real AdMob ad during E2E – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

Claude Code tapped a real AdMob ad during E2E

Our AdMob test-device setup applied only to debug builds, so a Claude Code agent testing a release APK on a real phone saw live ads and clicked one of them once.

A Claude Code agent was tapping through an Android app on a real phone when an interstitial ad came to the front, and its next tap landed on the ad. AdMob counts live impressions and clicks on a developer's own device as invalid traffic.

The setting that sends test ads to our development phones applied only to debug builds, so the release APK served live ads. The agent's screen-check guard read only the package name, so it took an ad screen opened inside the app for the app itself, and the tap that hit the ad never went through that guard at all. The next day the setting went into every build, but banners inside our own screens and ads from other networks are still not fully covered.

Chrome opened from behind an interstitial

On the afternoon of September 28, 2026, the agent installed a release APK of our Korean spell checker SugarSpeller on a Galaxy S21 and walked through the whole check flow. Its script force-stopped the app and relaunched it through a share intent for every check.

One agent command dumped the screen, read the coordinates of the result bubble and sent a tap there. The tap landed at 16:19:55, when the dump finished, and a tenth of a second later logcat showed Chrome opening a shopping advertiser's page. When the agent dumped the screen again, the script stopped with "foreground is not our app": Chrome's first-run screen was in front.

After Chrome was closed, an interstitial in the Google Mobile Ads SDK's AdActivity was still up inside the app. The agent wrote that it would close the ad with BACK only and never tap it. After BACK, a second ad screen was underneath, from another ad network, Liftoff (formerly Vungle). Twenty-nine minutes later it told the operator it had clicked a real ad once, an invalid click, and recorded the same in the changelog's incident line.

The guard only checked the package name

At 14:56 that day the agent had added a guard to its screen dump and screenshot script. It read the topResumedActivity line, the activity in front, and carried on if the app's package name appeared there. Ad SDK screens run inside the app's process, so that line reads like com.sugarmount.sugarspeller/com.google.android.gms.ads.AdActivity and passes. The guard also sat only in front of the dump and screenshot commands; the tap that clicked the ad was a raw command that never went through it.

The guard changed twice within two minutes of the click.

TimeRuleWhat happened
14:56 (v1)Continue if the app's package name is on the front-screen lineAd screens passed. Taps ran outside the guard
16:20 (v2)Stop if the name contains AdActivity or gms.ads; move taps into the script, only with numeric coordinates more than 250 px below the topAfter BACK, Liftoff's VungleActivity underneath was not on the name list
16:21 (v3)Continue only if the front screen is one of the app's own classes; otherwise stop and close with BACKAt 16:44 it blocked a tap in front of a Liftoff ad

The v2 assumption was that ad screens can be recognized by name. With mediation, where several ad networks bid for the same slot, each network brings its own screen name, and an unlisted one appeared 13 seconds after v2 went in. v3 lists what is allowed instead of what is blocked. The agent also removed the force-stop from each check that day, because every relaunch showed an app-open ad.

The test-device list was wired to debug builds only

The app had a test-device list in code, but a September 11 fix applied it only inside a BuildConfig.DEBUG check, which is true only in debug builds. A release APK on a real phone skipped the list entirely, and the S21 was not on it anyway.

The next night, while instrumentation tests (Android tests that launch the app on the phone itself) ran on the S21, the operator asked whether the account would get suspended, since ads kept showing during testing. The agent first answered that the instrumentation tests were debug builds using test ad units, so there was no risk. That was wrong. This app's debug build deliberately uses the real ad units so the bidding partners can be verified, and a comment in the same file said so. The logcat the agent then checked had three copies of the SDK hint that only unlisted devices get: call setTestDeviceIds to get test ads on this device.

Twenty-seven minutes after the question, commit ec5f400 moved the call out of the debug condition. Only listed devices get test ads, so real users are unaffected. The commit added the S21 and a unit test checking that the S21 is on the list and that the configuration carries the whole list.

The two days of developer-phone testing also show in AdMob reporting. When we pulled daily banner requests again, September 29 alone had more than twice the usual thousand or so requests, and the match rate (the share of ad requests that actually got an ad) fell below half.

Our October 1 monitoring note says all of the extra requests came from version 1.6.024 and puts them down to the S21 and S23 running instrumentation tests against real ad units. In the raw data, every unmatched request on September 28 and 29 but one came from that version too. That version number was shared by the development builds and the Play release at the time, so the version alone does not single out the devices.

The S23 was on the list and still got live ads. Resetting a phone's advertising ID also changes the test-device value the SDK uses, and the code still held the value from before the reset. The agent said the test-device ID is the MD5 of the advertising ID and computed it, but the result did not match the log, and neither did an MD5 of the Android ID. On the operator's instruction, the code got the value the SDK printed in logcat.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

We put the test-device list in every build and the console

Five fixes came up. The agent objected to two from the operator's side, and the operator stopped the build flag the agent was writing.

OptionRaised byOutcome
Turn the app's debug constant on for testing and off for releaseOperatorAgent objected: the constant also forces a premium subscription, and forgetting to turn it off would give every user test ads and free premium
Build flag for test ad units that fails the Play upload (AAB) build if left onAgentOperator stopped it mid-test and switched to console registration. Never built (not in the repository as of November 18)
Switch the debug build to test ad units(Sep 11 review)Dropped: test units skip mediation, so bidding partners can't be verified
Watch a few live ads to check, then shipOperator questionAgent objected: live impressions and clicks on a developer device are invalid traffic at any count
Apply the code list to every build and register devices in the consoleAgent, operatorChosen. Code in ec5f400; console registration left to the operator

On the morning of September 30 the operator asked whether the S21 was registered as an AdMob test device too. The agent said only in code. The code list only covers builds that contain it. If an older version from Play is installed on a developer phone, only the test-device registration in the AdMob console protects it. The console takes the raw advertising ID and the code takes the SDK hash, so both values went into a per-device table in the repository docs (4595dce).

An ad ID file copied into a worktree

About a week later the same risk came in by another route in our puzzle game Arrow Knots. The game keeps its real ad IDs in one settings file that git ignores, and a release build uses the file whenever it exists. At 01:28 on October 4, the Claude Code session handling ads got the IDs from the operator and, without asking, copied the file into another session's working folder (a git worktree). Twenty-one minutes later that session built what it took to be a test release APK.

At 02:06 that session passed on the ad session's warning that random-tap testing must never run on a real-ID build, wrote that its own workspace had no real-ID file and would build with test ads only, so it was safe, and then installed the APK on an S20. A file check in the same command printed that the file was there. The session uninstalled the app without ever opening it, moved the file aside, and rebuilt with test ads. No ad request or click happened.

The game's test-ads flag only allowed test IDs when the file was missing; it did not ignore a file that was present. Commit 68d501e the next day made the build read the file from its original location through a build argument, so a worktree never needs a copy. Our block puzzle, built in the same days, has a test-ads flag that ignores the file entirely; what its real-ID check still missed is in Why R8 kept 5 AdMob test IDs in a release AAB.

The September 30 check still logged the Liftoff app-open ad as live

The tap guard only checks whether the front screen is one of our activities, so it cannot see a banner or native ad placed inside our own screen. If coordinates happen to land on a banner, the guard lets the tap through. That is why the order below puts test-device registration ahead of the tap rule.

The code list only covers AdMob ads. At 08:57 on September 30 the operator said the console registration was done, but the records do not say which consoles or which devices. In the S21 check that followed, AdMob served test ads; the Liftoff app-open ad was still live and did not close with BACK, so the app was force-stopped to close it. The session judged it live from what was on screen and asked the operator to recheck the test-device setting in the Liftoff dashboard.

Register test devices before any device E2E

Do not run automated taps on a real device with any build that can serve live ads. This is the order we put together from this incident. Of these, using the logcat value and applying the list to every build (steps 1 and 2) are already in the app repository's rules, and tapping only on our own screen (step 5) and never copying the real-ID file into another worktree (step 6) are already in the agent's memory.

  1. Connect the device, launch the app once, and copy the value from the setTestDeviceIds(Arrays.asList("…")) line in logcat. Don't compute it.

  2. Add that value to the app's test-device list and keep the MobileAds.setRequestConfiguration call outside any build-type condition. Add a unit test that checks the device is on the list.

  3. Register the same phone's raw advertising ID as a test device in the AdMob console and in each mediation partner's console.

  4. Relaunch the app, check that ads carry the test-ad label, and confirm the "to get test ads on this device" line no longer shows in logcat.

  5. Inside the tap script's tap command, tap only if the activity name from adb shell dumpsys activity activities | grep -m1 topResumedActivity starts with one of the app's own classes, such as <package>/.; otherwise send BACK. Relaunch the app only when you must.

  6. Keep the real ad ID file in one place and pass its path to the build. Never copy it into another session's worktree.

  7. The next day, check match rate and request counts in the AdMob report. Leaked developer-device traffic shows there first.

Random-tap crash hunting is in VIBRATE crash and the fresh-install monkey test; we run that only on test-ad builds as well.

As of 2026-11-18. App repository git history (ec5f400, 536ce09, 4595dce, ff7a5aa; changelog entries for Sep 28 and Sep 30), game repository git history (68d501e) and agent memory, Claude Code session logs (Sep 28 to 30, Oct 4), and banner request and matched-request counts pulled again from the AdMob Network Report API (2026-11-18).

item.title: Play Console in-app price VAT: 7,500 became 8,000 – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Short note

Play Console in-app price VAT: 7,500 became 8,000

The Korea price field in Play Console takes the amount before VAT, so typing KRW 7,500 for our one-time in-app product made the buyer price 8,000 won.

We typed 7,500 won into Play Console, and the next day the Pro price on the app's settings screen read 8,000. This was October 2026, while setting up the one-time Pro purchase for SugarDoc, our viewer for Korean HWP documents. The AI coding agent had guessed the field was tax-inclusive, while the owner's first take, that Play adds 10% to the console price, was the right one.

We sent 6,900 and Play stored 7,500

On October 5 a Claude Code agent created the product through the Play Developer API (Google's API for doing Play Console work from code) and sent the owner's chosen price of 6,900 won. Reading the product back, the Korea price was 7,500. The agent took that for a conversion bug and tried to overwrite it with 6,900; the auto-mode permission classifier blocked the edit because it changes what real buyers pay.

The owner answered on the spot that 6,750 in the console would come to 7,500 for buyers once Play added 10%. The agent replied that 6,750 plus 10% is 7,425, so the numbers did not match, and labeled as a guess that the stored 7,500 was probably already the tax-inclusive buyer price. In the same reply it explained 7,500 as 6,900 plus 10% (7,590) rounded down to a price point, yet left rounding out when it checked the owner's 6,750. The owner typed 7,500 into the console, and the agent updated the docs from the owner's message without reading the stored price again.

On October 6 the on-device end-to-end (E2E) report caught 8,000 won on the settings screen. The app never hard-codes a price; it shows whatever Play returns, so the console value went straight to the screen.

On October 8 the agent put the two input and stored pairs side by side and wrote that its tax-inclusive guess had been wrong. The owner typed 5,000, the Korea price the API returned was 5,500, and the agent fixed the docs within the same minute.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The conversion API takes a pre-tax price and returns a taxed one

Google Play's help page on tax rates lists South Korea among the countries where the price shown to buyers must include tax. The API reference for convertRegionPrices describes its input price as "Tax exclusive" and each converted region price as "tax inclusive."

Write down the price you read back

Since the classifier block on October 5, the owner changes prices in the console and the agent only reads them.

  1. Take the Korea price you want buyers to pay and divide by 1.1; that goes in the console (5,000 for 5,500). If the result is not a round number, the stored price may be moved to a nearby price point.

  2. After saving, read the buyer price from the product GET's regionCode KR entry or from the store listing.

  3. Record both numbers, for example "buyer 5,500 won (console 5,000)."

  4. If you create products through the conversion API, note in a code comment that its input is pre-tax.

Update a documented price only from the value you read back after saving. A different Play API result we failed to check before acting is in Play staged rollout API: 20% went out as 100%.

These records cover one one-time product in October 2026; we have not checked subscriptions or accounts that file Korean VAT themselves as a local business. The console path, where 7,500 typed in became 8,000, is something we observed; we could not confirm from the help pages that the same rounding rule applies there. The product script overwrites only the Korea price with the buyer price, while converting every other region from that same number as if it were pre-tax, so other regions may be priced higher than intended. We have not rerun it to check.

As of 2026-11-18. Sources: app repository git history (commit 2cc25d1, PRD and implementation plan), agent session logs (2026-10-05 to 10-08), a read-only Play Developer API query, Google Play Console Help and the Android Publisher API reference.

item.title: Claude Code Android: a build gate for zero ads – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Claude Code Android: a build gate for zero ads

The zero-ads gate Claude Code built had to read both the release dependency graph and the merged manifest; with the dependency check alone, a build carrying AD_ID passed.

An Android app that ships no ad SDK at all can still request the advertising ID permission. HWP Viewer SugarDoc, our viewer for Korean word-processor files, was built with no ads by decision. Firebase Analytics, which it uses for statistics, pulls in four libraries that declare AD_ID, and the manifest merger copies that into the app. Left alone, the Play Console listing says "no ads, no advertising ID" while the AAB asks for it.

The first gate a Claude Code agent wrote looked only at the dependency graph, and a review agent caught the hole. When we reran the same repository in a throwaway folder on November 18, 2026, a gate that checks dependencies alone passed a build whose merged manifest still had AD_ID.

The first gate checked dependencies only

The three photo apps in the same repository show banner, interstitial and app-open ads. When the viewer started, the agent offered two ad plans (no ad SDK, or one home-screen banner), and early on October 5 (Korea time) the operator picked no ads. The app's config file got one line, adsMode=NONE.

About two hours later an implementing agent built the gate. The release config task verifyReleaseConfig gained rules that every ad id field must be empty and that the release dependency graph must not contain Google Mobile Ads (GMA, Google's ad SDK) or its consent SDK (UMP). The app manifest got four tools:node="remove" lines that strip the advertising-id permissions, and two unit tests reading the merged release manifest guarded those lines.

The workflow instructions said to remove each new guard for a moment and confirm a test fails, and the agent ran several deliberately broken copies. Copies that added an ad id or an ad module were run through verifyReleaseConfig, the task the AAB build depends on; the copy with the remove lines deleted was run through unit tests only and never through that task.

Four review agents started as soon as the implementer finished. The one assigned to rules and gates wrote: "bundleRelease depends on only one gate, verifyReleaseConfig, and it checks the dependency graph but not the merged manifest." Delete the remove lines, build and upload, and the store declares no advertising ID while the AAB has it. The reviewer filed it as minor and noted that the manifest unit tests ran only from the release script, never from the AAB build command.

A fix agent spent about 20 minutes moving the rules into a separate file and adding the merged-manifest check to the same task. Later that morning the operator asked again whether the app really had no ads at all, then set both the ads and advertising-ID answers in Play Console's app content section to "no". The gate, fix included, landed in the repository with commit ca1ade4 on October 8; the dependency-only version was never committed.

How Firebase puts AD_ID back

The viewer's telemetry module depends on Firebase Analytics. In the release dependency graph we pulled again on November 18, firebase-analytics 23.2.0 brings a set of measurement libraries, and among them is play-services-ads-identifier 18.0.0, the library that reads the advertising ID.

The manifest merger report says which library added each permission. With the remove lines gone, AD_ID was declared by four libraries, and two of them added two permissions from Android's newer ad-measurement APIs (AdServices). ACCESS_ADSERVICES_TOPICS, which the app manifest also removes, is declared by nothing in this version; the merger only warned that there was nothing to remove.

The dependency check stays silent because play-services-ads-identifier is not on its deny list. Adding it would block Firebase Analytics itself, so a code comment says it is not an ad SDK and leaves it out on purpose. Permissions live in the manifest, so a check that reads only the dependency list cannot see this path.

Widening the deny listWhat happens with today's graphWhy not
Deny play-services-ads-identifier tooAlways fails, Firebase Analytics brings itStatistics would have to go
Fail on any module named adsads-identifier and privacysandbox ads-adservices match via FirebaseFalse positives
Check config values onlyConfig is clean in state D, where the ad module is addedMisses an ad module coming in
Make bundleRelease depend on all release unit testsThe reviewer's second suggestionNo reason for not picking it is on record

When the remove lines go away, four Firebase libraries add AD_ID again, the dependency check stays quiet because those libraries are allowed, and the tests that read the manifest sit outside the AAB build path. The fix agent cut the last link: the merged-manifest check now runs inside verifyReleaseConfig, so bundleRelease fails even with the first three in place.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

One app, four states

Without touching the source repository, we unpacked origin/main into a temporary folder and ran the viewer's verifyReleaseConfig four times. The Firebase config file was the fake template the repository ships (without it, every run adds a "google-services.json is missing" line).

StateChangeResultAD_ID in merged manifest
Anonepassno
Bfour remove lines deletedfail, 3 manifest linesyes
CB, plus the manifest check call removedpassyes
Dthe photo apps' ad module addedfail, 3 dependency + 12 manifest linesno

C is close to the gate as first built on October 5: the advertising-id permission is in, and the build succeeds. D goes the other way. The remove lines are intact, so AD_ID is stripped, but the ad SDK, UMP and the WorkManager library the ad SDK pulls in trip the dependency rule, and the manifest rule catches one ad activity and eleven WorkManager components. B is caught only by the manifest check; D trips both layers.

In the same copy, with the manifest check call removed, we also ran the rule tests (./gradlew -p build-logic test). All 15 passed. The tests guard the rule functions; nothing tests that the task calls them.

Wiring both checks into one task

This can live in a convention plugin (a Gradle build-config plugin shared by several modules) or in an app module's build.gradle.kts. Our repository keeps it in the convention plugin every app applies and switches it on with adsMode in each app's config file.

  1. Give the app config an ads mode. With NONE, pass only when every ad id is empty and every ad flag is false.

  2. Walk the release runtime graph (releaseRuntimeClasspath) to the end, collect each external module's group:name, and compare against exact names. Our list has seven: four Google ad SDK artifacts, UMP and two WorkManager artifacts. play-services-ads-identifier is not on it.

  3. Strip the advertising-id permissions in the app manifest.

    <uses-permission android:name="com.google.android.gms.permission.AD_ID" tools:node="remove" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_ADSERVICES_AD_ID" tools:node="remove" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_ADSERVICES_ATTRIBUTION" tools:node="remove" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_ADSERVICES_TOPICS" tools:node="remove" />

  4. In the same task, read the release variant's merged manifest and fail on AD_ID or ACCESS_ADSERVICES_* permissions, GMA meta-data, or GMA, UMP and WorkManager components. This is the step that catches step 3 disappearing. The permission part, taken from the repository:

    // plugin: hand the release variant's merged manifest to the task as an input
onVariants(selector().withBuildType("release")) { variant ->
    mergedReleaseManifest.set(variant.artifacts.get(SingleArtifact.MERGED_MANIFEST))
    releasePackage.set(variant.applicationId)
}
// rule function: match permission names
(elements("uses-permission") + elements("uses-permission-sdk-23")).map { it.name() }
    .filter { it == "com.google.android.gms.permission.AD_ID" || it.startsWith("android.permission.ACCESS_ADSERVICES_") }
    .forEach { problems += "adsMode=NONE but the merged manifest requests $it" }

  5. Make the AAB task depend on it.

    tasks.matching { it.name == "bundleRelease" }.configureEach { dependsOn(verifyReleaseConfig) }

  6. Move the rules into functions with no Gradle types and give each rule a "break it and it fails" unit test. Then run the real project in states A to D and confirm A and C pass while B and D fail; of the broken states, only C should pass.

  7. Find which library adds a permission in build/outputs/logs/manifest-merger-release-report.txt, and what pulls it in with ./gradlew :app:dependencies --configuration releaseRuntimeClasspath.

Don't write the lists from memory. Pull your dependency graph and merger report once; those two outputs are where the lists in steps 2 and 4 come from.

Ad SDKs off the list, and wiring without a test

The gate knows only Google's ad SDKs. The dependency list is seven exact module names, and the manifest prefixes cover GMA, UMP and WorkManager. Another ad network's SDK would pass both layers. We have not tried one in the viewer.

Blocking WorkManager works because the viewer uses none (it even cleans its document inbox without it). An app that needs scheduled work would have to change that line first. The gate hangs off bundleRelease only, so assembleRelease, which builds a release APK, does not run it.

Whether the task calls the rule functions is covered today by the release unit tests the release script runs. They read the same merged manifest, but the AAB build command alone does not run them. Next is pinning state C as a build-logic test, so that deleting the call fails a test.

A gate in another app whose input itself differed from the release is covered in Our release gates were checking something other than the release; here the input was the same build, and the gate skipped its manifest layer. The photo apps' full gate order is in AI-built Android app release checklist.

As of 2026-11-18. Session and workflow records from Oct 4-5 (implementer, reviewer and fixer agent reports), app repository git history (the Oct 8 commit that carried the gate), Gradle output and manifest merger report rerun in a throwaway copy.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

  • Play Console in-app price VAT: 7,500 became 8,000
  • A month of 'temporary error': our subscription details screen never waited for products, and 1 of 16 users started checkout
  • Play Store title keywords: two weeks, no verdict
  • Four Google Ads app campaigns, $36.4, 105 installs, about 3% ROAS: CPI ran 30 times break-even
