item.title: Game feel fix: a heart that fell 109 ms early – SugarMount
item.description:
AX Notes · Method

Mobile game feel: frame timing showed our heart penalty landing 109 ms before the collision

Don't stop at asking an agent to fix the animation. Give it the code and the recording's frames, and have it list each event's cause and effect in order. Use timing measurements to prove the fix.

When players say a game has no feel, the cause is often not missing effects but events landing in the wrong order. In Arrow Knots, our then-unreleased puzzle game, tapping a blocked arrow made the heart drop first; the arrow reached its blocker 109 ms later. The effect came before its cause.

On the night of October 1, 2026, when the operator called the animation sloppy, the AI agent committed 719 lines of new effects within 11 minutes and the order stayed wrong. It changed only after a code and frame review that asked, event by event, what causes what and in which order. In the recording after the fix, the heart moves 16 ms after contact. Below: how to measure a recording, and what to tell the agent.

Measured again, the heart led by 109 ms

The recordings from before and after the fix each hold one blocked tap. We decoded both frame by frame, counted pixels whose brightness changed by more than 25 between frames, split the count into the header and the board, then checked the result against contact sheets by eye. The median frame gap was about 8 ms, which set the resolution. A 60 Hz screen would limit it to about 17 ms.

EventBefore (level 151)After (level 52)
Arrow starts moving3,807 ms3,851 ms
Heart starts changing3,815 ms3,984 ms
Contact (board shake before, contact ring after)3,924 ms3,968 ms
Heart relative to contact109 ms early16 ms late

Before the fix, the heart began to swell 8 ms after the arrow set off and had faded about halfway by the time anything touched. The review document describes this scene as the effect coming before the cause. That night the reviewer printed time-stamped 60 fps frame differences, and the output showed the heart changing at 3.817 s and the board at 3.933 s, but the review document recorded no measured value. The 109 ms was measured from the original frames a month after the fix.

In the fixed code, the contact callback runs before the ring is drawn. The 16 ms in the video is about two frames, so read it as the delay until each change reaches the screen. Nobody tuned it to that value.

A 719-line rewrite left the order alone

At 22:05 the operator's verdict, roughly, was that the animation was too sloppy for anyone to bother playing. The agent assumed the game lacked effects. It added snake-like exits, five synthesized sound effects, vibration, confetti and a star card, and committed it at 22:16.

It had looked at frames too: 89 at 5 fps, then 162 and 149 at 10 fps, recorded on the S21. Its notes from that pass say the blocked bump and the heart animation checked out. Nothing in the log times their order. What it changed afterward was the result backdrop, the confetti and the coloring of touching arrows. The report said the work was checked frame by frame. In the rewritten code the heart still dropped at the moment of the tap.

About fifteen minutes later the operator told it to analyze more deeply. The agent split the work into three tracks, and the game-feel reviewer came back in 4 minutes 51 seconds with 6 problems seen on video and 14 recommendations.

The heart code sat one line after the animation call

bump launches its animation in a coroutine and returns immediately, so the next two lines run in the same frame that handles the tap.

is TapResult.Blocked -> {
    fx.bump(id, distance, r.blockers)  // starts the animation, returns at once
    lives = state.lives                // heart drops at the tap
    feedback.blocked(view)             // sound and vibration at the tap
}

One level down, state.tap() settled the outcome on the spot and the UI code sat right there, so nothing separated rule time from display time.

The poke that sends a blocked arrow to its blocker took longer with distance: (90 + 45 * distance).toInt().coerceAtMost(260). The review document put contact 90 to 260 ms after the tap; those are the two ends of this formula. Distance is k + 0.55, so a real blocked tap takes at least about 114 ms. The recording showed 117 ms. This tap sits near the formula's shortest case; by the formula, a far-blocked arrow would have widened the reversal to nearly 260 ms.

The reviewer was asked a different question

The blocked-tap behavior the first pass approved came back as a problem in the review. The reviewer also cut the same video into 149 frames at 10 fps. Its brief asked for motion timing and easing per event, feedback layering per event (visual, audio, haptic), and any abrupt cuts visible frame by frame.

At 10 fps, frames are 100 ms apart, so a 109 ms gap is a single step. The reviewer read the code first, skimmed the 149 frames, then recut only the blocked-tap section at 30 and 60 fps.

The review document pinned the reversed order on code lines and cited no frame numbers for it. An arrow flying over the hearts and status bar (frames 58, 62 and 89), the opening pop-in hidden by the splash fade (frame 21), and a red warning tint that barely showed on the vermilion arrow all came from frames. Take call order and the timing of sound and vibration from the code; take what shows on screen and the actual timestamps from the frames.

The rule stayed instant; only the display moved

Delaying the rule result until contact was an option, but the review said to keep it immediate and the build followed. The document doesn't give a reason. bump gained an onContact callback, and heart, sound and vibration moved inside it.

fx.bump(id, dist, r.blockers) {        // called when the poke lands
    feedback.contact(view, costsLife = !tutorial)
    if (!tutorial) lives = state.lives
}

The poke became a fixed 110 ms instead of scaling with distance, so contact no longer shifts with distance. The poke in these two taps took 117 ms both before and after; what moved was the heart. Board shake dropped from 0.12 of a cell to 4 dp, and red now appears only in the contact ring. The blocked arrow darkens and its blocker gets a white outline.

Under rapid taps, lives = state.lives in the callback jumped straight to the final count, and a fix the next morning made it drop one heart per contact. That incident has its own note: Rapid taps and an unlocked Retry button.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Eight colors became six

The review measured color as well, using the Machado 2009 simulation matrices with the CIEDE2000 color-difference formula, and treated a difference under 10 as hard to tell apart. We implemented the formula separately on November 4, 2026, and every value matched.

VisionOld 8 colors, smallest differenceNew 6 colors, smallest difference
Typical12.822.5
Protan5.517.0
Deutan7.416.7
Tritan2.718.5

Against the paper background, amber reached 2.43:1 and green 2.9:1, both under the 3:1 in WCAG 1.4.11. The warning red and the vermilion arrow differed by 11.1 for typical vision but only 2.0 under tritan simulation, so blocked state ended up carried by shape and motion. The review judged that making all eight colors safe for color vision deficiency was close to impossible, and noted that six colors are enough because the neighbor graph is planar.

To fix contrast the review recommended darkening amber to B87A00, which made things worse: it cuts the deutan difference from vermilion from 7.4 to 2.4. The reviewer saw that number in its own 22:35 run and left the advice in. The agent doing the implementation searched six-color combinations and replaced the whole palette. That search missed the review's target of 20, and 16.7 became the accepted minimum.

Following the review crashed the first tap

Recommendation 14 said to replace weak vibration on Samsung devices with VibrationEffect.Composition. It didn't mention permissions, and the commit that applied the review shipped the change without declaring VIBRATE, so the first arrow to leave the board threw SecurityException.

At 22:46 the agent had a tutorial script finish without a crash, and on the S24 it had only confirmed install and launch. Asked whether testing was done, it said no. About four minutes later the operator found the tutorial error by hand on that S24. A monkey run on an S21 from fresh state died at event 15 of 800. At 22:47 a level-check script had removed 16 arrows on the same code without dying. The logs don't settle why either script missed it.

The next commit declared the permission and made vibration failures fall back to standard haptics. Three seeds of 800 events each on the S21 gave zero fatal errors. Right after that, the fresh-state monkey run became a script.

Record a blocked tap, fill the table, fix, fill it again

  1. Record a level on a real device, with every event in it at least once: blocked, removed, cleared.
  2. Cut the whole clip at 10 fps, number the frames on a contact sheet, and show the agent.
  3. Have the agent read the code too, and tell it: "For each event, give me a table of cause frame, effect frame, and where sound and vibration are called. Find where an effect comes before its cause. Mark each number as a code formula or a video measurement." Leave "make it better" out of the brief.
  4. Recut only the suspect section at 60 fps to look at it, and read times from the original frames' timestamps.
  5. After the fix, record the same scene, fill in the same table, and run monkey from fresh state, as in the fresh-install monkey test note.
adb shell screenrecord --time-limit 25 --bit-rate 8000000 /sdcard/run.mp4
adb pull /sdcard/run.mp4
ffmpeg -i run.mp4 -vf fps=10,scale=360:-1 f_%04d.png
ffmpeg -ss 3.6 -t 0.9 -i run.mp4 -vf fps=60,scale=360:-1 g_%03d.png

Replace -ss 3.6 -t 0.9 with the time of the blocked tap in your own video. The code below prints each frame's time and, for the header and board regions, how many pixels changed in brightness by more than 25. Region ratios differ per game.

import cv2
c = cv2.VideoCapture("run.mp4")
H = int(c.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT)); prev = None
while True:
    ok, f = c.read()
    if not ok: break
    t = c.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_POS_MSEC)
    g = cv2.cvtColor(f, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    if prev is not None:
        d = cv2.absdiff(g, prev) > 25
        print(round(t), d[int(H*.04):int(H*.1)].sum(), d[int(H*.12):int(H*.8)].sum())
    prev = g

The table above came from decoding every original frame with OpenCV: 1,276 before the fix and 1,840 after. No frames arrive while the screen is still. Gaps in these recordings had a median of 8 ms and a maximum of 3 seconds, so never convert frame numbers to time.

Sound, haptics, fingers and long sessions stay off camera

Sound didn't make it into the screen recording, and video can't show vibration strength. Automated taps hit the exact center of a cell, so they say nothing about real finger accuracy. Long-session defects are missed as well: this game's spring-back crash appeared 28 times in a 300-level stress run the next day.

The boards being too easy was already flagged in the rewrite report, and separate level analysis measured and fixed it the same night. The generator side is covered in A reverse-construction generator and the gate behind 1,100 arrow-puzzle levels.

Far-blocked taps and retention weren't measured

An arrow blocked from far away wasn't timed. We have no player metric, such as retention, comparing game feel before and after.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Frequently asked questions

How many milliseconds should game feedback animation take?

This game fixes the poke at 110 ms and puts heart, sound and vibration in the contact callback. We haven't validated those values for any other game.

What frame rate should I use to review a recording?

Use 10 fps to skim and 60 fps to look at a section, and read times from the original frames. This recording averaged 85.58 fps.

Is a debug build good enough for this?

It was enough to find the order; both recordings here are debug builds. We didn't repeat the measurement on a release build, so use one if you also want to compare frame delays.

Checked 2026-11-04. The game repository's git history and review document, and that night's agent session logs. The 109 ms and 16 ms figures were remeasured from the original recordings. Clock times are Korea time.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • We slowed a mini game down twice before checking why it was hard: players couldn't recall the answers
  • A reverse-construction generator and the gate behind 1,100 arrow-puzzle levels
  • Block puzzle difficulty: how simulation bots caught a game you could never lose
  • Rapid taps and an unlocked Retry button: a 600 ms result-card lock, and the 28 crashes a stress run found next
  • GA4 custom dimension (not set) for numeric params
  • Seven edited HWP files in Hancom's Android apps: 7 of 7 opened, and the re-save waited for a human sign-in

item.title: Why we replaced an app privacy policy template – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Retrospective

App privacy policy templates: we threw ours out and rewrote it from a code audit

Four apps shared one generated privacy policy. We replaced it with 8 pages written from source, each checked by a second agent looking for counter-evidence.

Plenty of first-time app makers fill in their privacy policy from a generator template. Four of our Android apps shared one such English template, which said user information "is not collected by me in any way", while one of them, the Korean spell checker SugarSpeller 1.6.025, was sending AI explanation requests and an anonymous ID to our own server.

On October 4, 2026, eight AI agents read the four codebases for 11 min 46 s and wrote 8 Korean and English policy pages. We treat a privacy policy as a code audit report first and a legal document second. Below: where the template was wrong, where the agents' drafts were wrong, and an audit order you can reuse. This note is not legal review.

Where the template and the 1.6.025 code disagreed

The template still ended with "created at privacypolicytemplate.net and modified/generated by App Privacy Policy Generator". It opened with a line ending "built the This app as a Free app." The word This sat where the app name belonged.

TemplateSugarSpeller 1.6.025 code
"retained on your device and is not collected by me in any way"AI explanation requests (corrected words up to 60 characters each, error type, checker, subscription status, app version) and a Firebase anonymous ID reach our server.
Two third parties: Google Play Services, AdMobNaver and Daum (Korean portals whose spell checkers do the checking), Firebase, Vertex AI (Gemini) and the ad partner Liftoff also receive data.
"Free app", "at no cost"Sells Google Play subscriptions.

1.6.025 was the first version to send data to our own server, but text to be checked had gone to Naver and Daum for longer than that, so the third-party list was already short. The design of the AI feature is in the first LLM in our spell checker.

We wrote down that it was wrong, and it stayed until October 4

At 21:49 on September 29, draft policy text and a Play Data safety answer table were committed to the SugarSpeller repository. The draft states that the published policy "is the template as is" and does not match reality. Step 3 of the release runbook says to fix the policy and the Data safety form before submitting the app.

When an agent fetched the Google Sites page at 11:05 on October 4, the paragraph was not there. 1.6.025 was rolling out by the night of October 1, so that version ran under the wrong policy for about two and a half days. The monitoring log counted 254 users on 1.6.025 between September 22 and October 3, with no note that test devices were excluded.

The agent's release notes on the night of September 29 said the policy had to change before submission, and on September 30 it handed the item back as the owner's third remaining task. Nothing records why the item stayed open, but the structure that allowed it is visible.

  1. The policy's sentences had no source in the code. A generator wrote them, so nothing could flag a mismatch when the code moved.
  2. The policy lived on Google Sites, outside any repository. Fixing it was one manual line in a runbook, and the four app repositories have no .github/workflows (checked November 4).
  3. Four apps shared one URL, as their Play listings showed. There was no page on which to state a fact about one app.

The one-paragraph plan rested on a sentence that did not exist

The September 29 plan kept the template and added a paragraph under "Information Collection and Use". The agent-written draft says the analytics and ads section could keep its "existing text (Google Analytics for Firebase, AdMob)". Searching the template for Analytics returns zero hits.

The paragraph would not have been enough anyway. On a shared page, a sentence about sending text to Naver would also have landed in the policy of SugarAlbum, a video maker, and "Free app" would have stayed.

The owner's request on October 4 was to move policies and app information to one site. Moving alone would have carried the same sentence to a new address. The audit was the agent's addition, and so was its size: 8 agents and about 1 million tokens excluding cache reads, which the agent reported as not requested.

One writer per app, one reviewer hunting counter-evidence

Four writer agents were told to "only claim what the code does" and, when unsure, to "disclose rather than deny". Four other agents then took the files, looked for evidence against every "we don't collect or send X" sentence, and fixed what was wrong. All four apps needed fixes.

AppWriter's draftAfter review
SugarSpellerSends words, error type and checker name to Vertex AIWords and error type only. The server passes original, corrected and type.
SugarCardNo ads while subscribedThe basic plan keeps the banner, and the exit-screen ad shows on every plan.
SugarAlbumThree groups of permissions missingAdded storage write, ad API and Firebase permissions after reading the merged release manifest.
SugarClipAndroid erases it beyond recoveryRemoved with app data or the app; backup copies are deleted in the Google account.

The first row claimed too much and the second flattered the app. These agents had the source open and the "only claim what the code does" instruction in front of them, and they still wrote those sentences. The workflow script had split writers from reviewers before any draft existed.

Reviewers also settled values that live outside the code. The SugarSpeller writer flagged that "deleted after 30 days" depended on a Firestore TTL policy it could not confirm. The reviewer read it from the API (ttlConfig.state: ACTIVE) and read retentionDays: 30 from the log bucket. That TTL was step 1 of the same runbook, also manual: a query at 16:00 on October 3 found it unset, and one at 01:00 on October 4 found it ACTIVE.

The numbers we deleted and the claim the owner dropped

On October 5 we put "Policies describe the actual code. Don't add claims the code doesn't back." into the site's agent instructions. On October 18 we added "If a fact cannot be verified there, leave it out."

An October 10 commit in our family calendar app AXFamily changed the invite link default from 72 hours to the 24 in the code, replaced "an internal ID instead of a name" with the fact that display names are sent, and deleted two numbers found nowhere in code or repository: "integrity tokens 12 hours" and "Play grace period 7 days". The same commit's move to the Seoul region turned out wrong, a story told in the AI processing notice we changed twice in a day.

On November 1 a person made the call. The Block Turn page promised no banner or interstitial in the first three games, but a classic game over counts as two runs, so an interstitial could appear from the second game over. The owner kept the code and removed the sentence, and the commit records it as an owner decision.

Policy work kept coming. After the new policies went up, through November 4, 22 of 104 commits have privacy, policy or the Korean word for it in the subject line, mostly policies for new apps. Across the whole repository it is 29 of 117. That is a subject-line grep, so one AX notes commit is in there by accident.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The same defect in a Play Data safety form on October 17

One more place states the same facts. At 14:41 on October 17, the owner asked whether Block Turn and Arrow Knots needed a Data safety fix. That day both public store pages listed four shared data types, but the collected section said no data was collected, while our site policies already listed Firebase Analytics and Crashlytics (added on October 8 and October 11).

The agent lacked console permission, so the owner entered the answers from a table, and at 14:58 the agent expanded the console preview and compared it line by line. On October 4, Play policy URLs couldn't be changed through the API either, so the owner changed four by hand. No app had the URL hard-coded, so that finished the move.

Nowhere to run a check between the four apps' code and a table

AXFamily goes further. Its processors live in processors.json, the policy tables are generated, and the CI job legal-consistency compares the output with the JSON and the in-app notice with the function constants. Its policy wasn't public on October 4, so we never compared the two side by side. We would still run the per-app audit on the four old apps.

Generating the tables alone could sit in the pre-commit check of the site repository, where the policies live. The hard part is comparing the JSON with app code: the four app repositories have no CI to run that, and SugarAlbum has had no commit since January 3. A per-app audit must be redone when the code changes; generation fails a check on a mismatch but needs somewhere in the app repository to run it. So far only AXFamily uses generation. Start any new app with it.

What reading the source cannot tell you, and legal review

  • Code can't confirm legal requirements. The section list came from a list of Korean privacy law items the agent wrote into its own prompt (purpose, items, retention, third parties and overseas transfers, destruction, user rights, privacy officer) plus earlier policies, and we have no record of a person or professional reviewing that list. The photo app policy the writers took their structure from on October 4 had no section on processors and overseas transfers; they added one, and the original got its own only 18 days later.
  • Source is not the shipped build. The SugarCard reviewer noted it could not tell which build was on Play, and SugarAlbum's merged manifest came from a January 3 build.
  • What an SDK collects isn't in the app's code. A September 23 commit added IP address, ad interactions and diagnostics to our first policy after the fact.

We haven't tried this on a service with many servers and processors, or on an outsourced app without source. We've only run it on Android apps with one operator.

Start by marking the negative claims in your published policy

If a sentence can't be tied to a line of code or a console value, delete it. Doubt "we don't collect" first.

  1. Fetch the published policy, split it into sentences and mark every negative claim.
  2. Note the app version and build a data flow table: data, destination, code location.
  3. Count permissions from the merged release manifest, not the source manifest. Permissions added by libraries appear only there.
  4. Read each SDK vendor's data disclosure and copy the items over.
  5. Read retention and deletion settings from the API instead of assuming them.
  6. Give the table and policy to a different agent or person and ask only for counter-evidence.
  7. Compare your Play Data safety answers with the same table.
  8. Record the audited commit next to the policy and run the diff below at each release. We have not done this step for the four apps.
# Permissions and dependencies changed since the audit
git diff $AUDITED HEAD -- '*AndroidManifest.xml' '*build.gradle*' '*libs.versions.toml'
# Permissions in the merged release manifest (path varies with AGP version)
grep -rh 'uses-permission' app/build/intermediates/merged_manifest/release/
# Firestore TTL and log retention
TOKEN=$(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "x-goog-user-project: $PROJECT" \
  "https://firestore.googleapis.com/v1/projects/$PROJECT/databases/(default)/collectionGroups/$GROUP/fields/$FIELD" \
  | grep -A3 ttlConfig
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "x-goog-user-project: $PROJECT" \
  "https://logging.googleapis.com/v2/projects/$PROJECT/locations/global/buckets/_Default" \
  | grep retentionDays

This diff does not see server code or request fields. SugarSpeller's repeated AI requests live under functions/, so these paths miss them. Add your server and network code paths.

Step 6 used a review prompt along these lines, shortened and with file paths removed.

Adversarially review the privacy policy pages against the real app source.
Read-only on the source repo. Check: every claim matches code (especially any
"we don't collect/send X" claims: look for counter-evidence: ad SDK, Firebase,
network calls, other paths), ko/en say the same thing.
FIX problems directly in those two files only.
Report: what you fixed, what remains uncertain.

The gate in our release gate and R8 crash note confirms the policy URL returns 200, which proves a page exists and says nothing about its sentences. The Firestore and logging calls copy the form the reviewer used on October 4; we did not rerun them for this note.

Four policies still dated October 4

All four policies still carry an effective date of October 4. In the repositories, SugarSpeller has reached 1.6.033, SugarCard 1.0.003 and SugarClip 1.2.002. A diff of SugarSpeller shows no new dependency in build.gradle, a manifest with queries for 3 sibling apps and one new game screen, and a server that can now send the same AI request up to 3 times. We haven't done the re-audit that decides whether any of this changes the policy.

The Play Data safety forms of those four apps have not finished being compared with these policies.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Is a privacy policy template risky for an app?

It is when its sentences differ from the code. Ours said "not collected by me" while the app sent data to our server. Use a template as a table of contents and rewrite the sentences from code.

Can an AI agent write my privacy policy?

It can draft one, but don't publish that draft unreviewed. All four of our source-based drafts needed fixes from a second agent. Keep writer and reviewer separate, and decide on professional review separately.

What do I write when I can't verify something?

Delete the claim or state it broadly on the side of disclosure. We deleted unsupported numbers such as "integrity tokens 12 hours", and kept a permission we could not tie to a build as "may be declared". Don't write a denial like "we don't store this" until you've checked.

Checked 2026-11-04. Git history of this site and the app repositories, work session records (September 29 to October 4, October 17), and SugarSpeller's release runbook and monitoring log. Not legal review; we do not judge whether our policies meet any statute.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: R8 renamed Gson fields: empty release results – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

203 unit tests missed a release-only blank result: R8 and Gson field names

A Gson field without @SerializedName stays at its default, with no exception, once R8 renames it, so the defect only shows up when you open the release artifacts.

Release-only bugs from R8 2/4

When R8 shortens field names in an Android release build, a Gson model without @SerializedName loses the link to its JSON keys and its fields stay empty. Nothing throws, and unit tests run on classes R8 never touched, so every test can pass while the release build is broken.

That was the state of the second spell-check path (the fallback taken when the first path fails) in our Korean spelling app SugarSpeller. On a release build it would have returned blank corrected text and zero errors, and all 203 unit tests were passing when we found it on September 14, 2026. Below are the cause, the test that now guards against it, and the commands that check the release artifacts directly.

Gson does not complain about a field it can't match

Without @SerializedName, Gson uses the Java field name as the JSON key. In the release build, R8 had done this to the Result response model:

# release mapping.txt just before the fix, 2026-09-14
output -> a
etype  -> b

The server still sends "output" and "etype". The object now has only a and b, so Gson skips both keys and the fields keep their initial "". Parsing succeeds, and the screen shows whitespace and zero errors.

Unit tests run against classes R8 never touched, so none of them ever saw a renamed field. The 203 is our recount of @Test annotations at the commit before the fix (the CHANGELOG says "200 or so"), and it includes tests that parse recorded server responses. The two fields had carried no annotation since the path was added on 2024-06-14. That path then stopped receiving responses at all, until a commit revived it on 2026-09-13. That commit and the fix shipped together in 1.6.017. We could not tell from the records whether users saw blank results while the path was alive earlier.

mapping.txt flagged 14 fields; two were defects

Finding it took 28 minutes. At 20:50 KST on September 14 the operator asked for a cross-check. The agent replayed the app's exact requests against the live servers (13 of 13 passed), then read the proguard rules and grew suspicious of model fields with no annotation. A script over the mapping.txt of a clean release build checked 19 model fields and listed 14 as renamed.

The same chart explains half of why the first spell-check path kept working in release: the keys holding its values were annotated. Why its unannotated message and result survived comes later. The fix at 21:18 annotated seven fields across both paths. No usable device was available that night, so "blank screen" was a verdict from mapping.txt and the dex files. We only saw the empty values at runtime later, in the reproduction below.

The agent's claim about debug builds lasted two days

Later that night the agent added an instrumented test and wrote in the commit message that because minify is on for debug too, the test runs in the same obfuscated state as the shipping build.

It was wrong, and that came out at 08:31 on September 16. The operator had opened KVM access so an Android 14 emulator could boot, and just before rerunning the test the agent checked whether the models were really obfuscated. Release said output -> a; debug kept the original name. The mapping.txt from October 9 shows the same. We did not establish why: the debug configuration.txt has no -dontobfuscate, though running the reproduction below with R8 --debug kept the names.

The agent then signed the release APK with the debug key, installed it, and blocked the first path's host in the emulator's hosts file to force the fallback. At 08:45 the second path's corrections appeared on the obfuscated build, and a commit fixed the docs at 08:47. The v16017 tag had already gone on at 07:47.

"lateinit got lucky" was really a keep rule

The fix commit has a wrong explanation of its own. Five unannotated lateinit fields kept their names, and the commit and the agent's memory file say R8 was keeping the names "by accident." While drafting this note in November we ran javap: Kotlin's lateinit var compiles to a public field, while var output = "" is a private field with a getter. The build at the time still had a rule meant for a Kakao SDK the app never used, -keepclassmembers class * { public static <fields>; public *; }, and that rule pinned every public field name. That rule was removed on September 25, as told in Play Console said our DEX was 39% optimized. The 1.6.026 mapping.txt has message -> a.

This is a reproduction, not the real app: a Java model of the same field visibility, shrunk with R8 9.4.14, Gson 2.14.0 and the proguard files from the fix commit, then parsed on the JVM.

AnnotatedConfigurationResult
NoneNo R8 (what unit tests see)Correct
NoneKakao rule + -dontobfuscate (stand-in for debug)Correct
NoneKakao rule (the September 14 release)output=[] etype=[], no exception
output, etype onlyKakao ruleCorrect
output, etype onlyKakao rule removedJsonIOException
All 5 fieldsKakao rule removedCorrect, message -> a

Row three reproduces the incident. Rows four and five show that annotating only output and etype would have passed on September 14, then broken eleven days later when the Kakao rule went away and message was renamed. Here the model is never constructed in code, so it ended in JsonIOException. When the code called the constructors and let the objects escape, both the September 14 configuration and the optimized one in use from September 20 ended in a NullPointerException. We did not build the real app, so we can't say which exception it would have thrown. The fix annotated the lateinit fields for the wrong reason and still got it right. Annotate every field that takes a value from JSON, lateinit or not.

Finding etype in the dex proves little

Before the fix, grep -a etype already hit classes2.dex and classes3.dex. classes4.dex, which held the model, did not have it, and that file gained it after the fix. The before-and-after in the fix commit was valid because it looked at that one file. But the AAB check that night and the pre-release check on September 16 looped over every dex and passed if etype appeared anywhere, and the report cited that as evidence. That loop would have passed the broken APK too.

Narrowing to one file no longer works either, since the 1.6.026 APK has a single classes.dex. We read all 43,818 strings in 1.6.026: 3 contain etype (a sentence with mimetype, closetype, and etype itself), 43 contain output, 97 contain message, 104 contain result.

dexdump -a from build-tools prints annotations with their values:

unzip -o app-release.apk 'classes*.dex' -d dex
dexdump -a dex/classes.dex | grep -c 'value="etype"'   # 1

The line reads VISIBILITY_RUNTIME Lkt1; value="etype". R8 renamed the annotation class to kt1 as well, so searching by class name finds nothing. Counted this way the release holds 11 spell-check keys in 13 annotations.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

An invariant test that fails when one annotation goes

The invariant test uses reflection to require an annotation on every field of the 8 response-model classes. This is the core, shortened:

private val models = listOf(Response::class.java, Response.Result::class.java)
private val codePopulated = setOf("com.example.Response#requestId")
@Test fun `every JSON field has SerializedName`() {
    val missing = models.flatMap { type ->
        type.declaredFields
            .filterNot { Modifier.isStatic(it.modifiers) || it.isSynthetic }
            .map { it to type.name + "#" + it.name }
            .filter { (_, key) -> key !in codePopulated }
            .filter { (f, _) -> f.getAnnotation(SerializedName::class.java) == null }
            .map { it.second }
    }
    assertTrue(missing.joinToString("\n"), missing.isEmpty())
}

The real file has three tests, adding a check of annotation values against JSON keys and a check that the exemption list codePopulated (10 entries today) holds no dead names. Before committing, the agent deleted the annotation on etype, watched this test and the key test end in FAILED, and restored it.

No package keep, and a debug device test can't see this

The broadest alternative is -keep on the whole model package. The fix did not add one, and the session has no record of weighing it. Judged now, the empty values would go away but safety would hang on one rule, and losing that rule would bring the incident back.

The instrumented test stayed, but on a debug build it can't see this defect. We have not tried setting testBuildType to release. A launch check doesn't help either: the R8 incident in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app was a crash at startup, and this one crashes nothing, so a cold start passes. The method behind our reproduction, shrinking the model with R8 --classfile under the app's proguard files and parsing on the JVM, showed the empty values with no device, but it is not in the repository.

Running the release APK through the whole path is the strongest evidence. On September 16 that session ran from 08:23 to 08:46, including other checks, and needed KVM access and a hosts-file block. So the invariant test runs with every test pass, and running the release APK stays a manual step in the docs for when a regression is suspected.

Auditing your own Gson models, from fromJson to the release APK

  1. rg 'fromJson|TypeToken|GsonConverterFactory' app/src/main lists what Gson fills. With Retrofit, follow the interface return types too.
  2. In the release mapping.txt, sort each renamed field into the three groups in the chart above (annotated, filled by code, defect).
  3. Add the invariant test, delete one annotation and confirm the failure.
  4. For each key, count value="key" in dexdump -a across all dex files and compare with the number of annotations in source. In 1.6.026 message appears twice, once per model, so accepting "at least one" would miss a lost annotation.
  5. Sign the release APK with the debug key, install it, and reach a screen that goes through that parser. A path behind a fallback only runs if you block the path in front of it.

What the test misses: new models and removed keep rules

models is a handwritten list, so a new response class is unchecked until someone adds it. The test only sees annotations on the source model; it passes if the keep rule protecting the annotation disappears or a class turns abstract. Step 5, running the release APK, is where those two show up. The two existing models stayed on Gson, while the explanation feature from The first LLM feature in a spell-check app takes its response as a Map and avoids this problem. We have not used a code-generating serializer.

Stale test comments and a dex check still done by hand

  • The test's header comment and the agent's memory still say that minified debug builds rename fields, and the memory also says lateinit survives by accident. Both need correcting.
  • The dex check in the docs is still a manual grep. It should become a dexdump -a value count in the release build script, with its key list taken from the test's expected values.
  • The only device on record that ran this path on an obfuscated build is the emulator. The next release should go through the fallback on real hardware.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Release-only bugs from R8: all 4 parts

  1. AI-built Android app release checklist: R8 and real devices
  2. R8 kept 5 AdMob test IDs in our release build: one listOf().any line and a dex count

FAQ

Do I still need keep rules if I use @SerializedName?

It depends on your Gson version. Gson 2.14.0, which this app uses, ships META-INF/proguard/gson.pro with rules that protect annotated fields, and our proguard-common.pro has a similar rule. In our local cache the 2.11.0 jar contains that file and the 2.10.1 jar does not, so open your own jar first.

Is "Abstract classes can't be instantiated" the same bug?

It comes from R8 too, but the symptom is different. In our reproduction, a top-level model with no annotated fields came out of R8 as an abstract class, and Gson threw JsonIOException. gson.pro protects <init>() on classes with @SerializedName fields, and annotating that class's fields made the error go away.

Sources: the app repository's git history and CHANGELOG, session logs, the 1.6.026 release APK and mapping.txt built on 2026-10-09, and a reproduction run on 2026-11-04 with R8 9.4.14.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Measuring 4.5:1 colour contrast in the site build – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

4.5:1 contrast in the site build: the dark hover pair that failed for 7 of 11 apps

A contrast rule that lives in one sentence of a doc does not hold. Our site build computes 11 contrast pairs per app and fails if any pair drops below 4.5:1.

Measuring text contrast 3/3

On a site where each app has its own accent colour, every colour change shifts the contrast of buttons, badges and link text along with it. This site started with one sentence as its rule: white text on the accent must reach 4.5:1. When we reworked the design system in October 2026 and measured again, the hovered outline button in dark mode fell below 4.5:1 for 7 of our 11 apps. Now the build computes 11 contrast pairs per app and fails if any falls short. Below: what that gate catches, what it still misses, and the steps to build the same gate.

Dark hover contrast at the October rework: 4.17 to 4.66

Each app on this site has a single accent hex in data/apps.json. sds_apps.py computes nine colour tokens from it as CSS text, and build.py writes that to a file. In dark mode the pale background bg-accent-weak is 24% accent mixed into the default dark surface #172131. The dark text colour fg-accent is the accent with its HSL lightness raised 1% at a time until it reaches 4.6:1 on #1D2940, the lightest of the three dark neutral surfaces.

Put fg-accent text on bg-accent-weak, as a hovered outline button would, and the 11 apps at the October 18 rework score: Arrow Knots 4.17, SugarSpeller 4.20, Compress Image 4.27, Flip & Rotate Image 4.31, SugarCard 4.40, SugarAlbum 4.41, AXFamily 4.41, Block Turn 4.58, SugarClip 4.59, Convert Image 4.64, SugarDoc 4.66. Seven are under 4.5 and nine under 4.6.

Our working notes say a review agent checking the design spec flagged this pair: "7 of 11 apps, lowest 4.17". We could not find the review itself, so we recomputed it from the app list at the rework and got the same numbers. The implementation commit already shipped the fixed pairing: in site.css, .button--outline:hover uses fg-accent-contrast for its text and border.

For 13 days the rule was one line of prose

The commit that first added the site pages, on 20 September 2026, set the default accent in site.css to #00897B ("default accent: SugarCompress"). The same day, the first commit of the utilities app repository listed "compress (temp) #00897B" in its design tokens. Both commits carry an AI co-author trailer. White text on that colour is 4.32:1, and the colour as text on the light background #F6F8FB is 4.06:1.

The next day, the "Design v2" commit in the utilities repository (also AI co-authored) caught it. Its design spec reads "temporary #00897B (4.3:1, fails AA) is replaced by #0F766E.", and another section makes 4.5:1 text contrast in both themes a principle. The site picked up #0F766E (white text 5.47:1) on 5 October, when a commit introduced data/apps.json.

The contrast rule that commit added to AGENTS.md was a field description: accent "(hex, white text on it must reach 4.5:1)". Searching that commit's tools/build.py for lumin, contrast or 4.5 finds nothing.

The first assumption matched the line: if white text clears 4.5:1 on the accent, the accent is safe. But one accent becomes nine tokens per theme, and those tokens meet as text and background in 11 pairs. Today every white-on-accent pair across the 13 apps is 5.45:1 or higher, while the dark hover pair from the same accents goes down to 4.17.

The dark accent was tuned against a different background

The dark hover used fg-accent for text and bg-accent-weak for the background. fg-accent only guarantees 4.6:1 on #1D2940 (relative luminance 0.0222), and for the blue and teal apps the pale background is lighter than that. Arrow Knots' bg-accent-weak, #14344E, has a luminance of 0.0315, and the same text colour #0A99EE falls from 4.71 to 4.17. The purple and magenta apps passed because their pale backgrounds sit close to #1D2940: Convert Image (#2C2359, 0.0246) at 4.64 and SugarDoc (#32223C, 0.0215) at 4.66.

A second assumption, made while writing this note, was that raising the target to 4.6 would cover the hover too, but the 4.6 target is measured on #1D2940, so with today's formula the pair on the pale background is still 4.17.

The fix is a token per pair. fg-accent-contrast takes the dark accent and lightens it again, 1% at a time, until it reaches 4.6:1 on the pale background. For Arrow Knots that moves #0A99EE to #17A2F5 and 4.17 to 4.61. The header of sds_apps.py states the rule as T2: "text on bg-accent-weak is fg-accent-contrast".

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The gate computes 11 pairs per app, 143 today

Inside python tools/build.py --check, which AGENTS.md says to run before every commit, sds_gates() checks three things. The rest of that check is described in Keeping a static site safe when several AI agents edit it: one --check before every commit.

  • for each app, 11 pairs; any pair under 4.5:1 is an error, SDS contrast <app>: <pair names>. Pairs have names like white on accent, accent on basement and d-contrast on d-weak; the full list of 11 is in audit();
  • the tokens read back from the generated assets/sds-apps.css must equal what accent_tokens() computes (rule T1: a literal hex per app);
  • the header mark colours in site.css must match the social-image generator og.py.

The docstring explains the 4.6 target: "targets are 4.6:1 so rounding and browser blending never drop below 4.5:1". Every mix and lightness step rounds RGB to integers. Because of that margin, Block Turn (4.58) and SugarClip (4.59) also got their own token, and in the dark block of the generated CSS at the rework, 9 of 11 apps declare a separate fg-accent-contrast.

We also ran a revert test. Setting Compress Image back to #00897B in the copy's apps.json made the gate print this (run with --check on 3 November, confirmed through audit() on 4 November):

error: SDS contrast sugarcompress: white on accent, accent on basement
1 gate error(s)

Two apps arrived later, CarDrawer (19 October) and TrimBox (31 October). Each added one hex to apps.json, and the colour code did not change through 4 November. The gate then computed 13 apps x 11 pairs = 143 pairs. As of 4 November, had the hover kept fg-accent, 9 of the 13 would have been under 4.5, with TrimBox at 4.22 and CarDrawer at 4.39.

Update, 13 November 2026: a site-wide colour refresh that day changed the dark neutral surfaces (the darkest is now #0E1217), and the tokens were recomputed by the same functions. After the refresh the lowest of the 143 pairs is AXFamily's dark accent text at 4.60:1. Had the hover kept fg-accent, 3 of 13 apps would now be under 4.5 (Compress Image and Arrow Knots at 4.39, Flip & Rotate Image at 4.48). Because the gate recomputes from the same formula, no colour had to be fixed by hand.

Swap the CSS pairing and the gate still passes

On 3 November we changed the site.css in a copy of the site so the hover text was var(--sds-fg-accent) again, rebuilt, and ran --check, which printed up to date; gates passed with the 4.17:1 pair back in the stylesheet. The only thing sds_gates() reads from site.css is the header mark regex; contrast comes entirely from the token pairs listed in audit().

As of 4 November, site.css used bg-accent-weak as the background in six rules.

SelectorText tokenIn the gate's pairs?
.app-tile:hoverfg-accent-contrastYes
.button--outline:hoverfg-accent-contrastYes
.badgefg-accent-contrastYes
.trust lifg-accent-contrastYes
[data-app] .notebody text fg-neutralNo
.ax-ctanot setNo

On app pages, .note keeps fg-neutral body text (its border, links and the eyebrow use fg-accent-contrast), and .ax-cta sets no text colour at all. Neither pair is among the 11, so neither is measured. We left both unfixed; that call belongs to whoever owns the build.

Both the mistakes and the catches in this history are recorded in AI co-authored commits or agent work. The spec rule that a new accent should be at least dE00 12 (a colour-distance measure) from existing ones was left out of the gate because "the new-key dE00 >= 12 rule needs a human to know which key is new"; the CLI only warns about pairs under dE00 8, currently 7 (smallest 2.2, Flip & Rotate Image and Arrow Knots).

color-mix() is banned by T3, and dark colours are not hand-picked

Letting the browser blend hover colours with CSS color-mix() is banned by rule T3. The gate compares literal hex values in the generated CSS with computed ones, and a browser-blended colour gives it nothing to compare. Hand-picking dark colours per app was dropped too: the site went from 11 apps to 13, and that approach means a person picking nine tokens for every new app.

We measured rendered pixels in another app; that write-up is Our contrast checker passed while skipping 40% of the text. sds_apps.py uses only the Python standard library and never starts a browser.

Without design tokens, with colours written per component, there is no pair list to compute in the first place. Gradients, text over photos and translucent layers don't reduce to two tokens, and this site doesn't measure them either.

From one accent hex to a 143-pair gate in six steps

  1. Keep one accent hex per brand or app in your source data and derive every other token with a function.
  2. Write down every text-on-background pair. Then search the CSS for rules that use each background token (grep -n "accent-weak" assets/site.css) and check each rule's text token against your list, as in the table above.
  3. Aim a little above 4.5 (we use 4.6), and give any pair that falls short its own token.
  4. Fail the build check when any pair is under 4.5:1, and compare the generated CSS values with the computed ones.
  5. Put an old failing colour into apps.json and run python tools/build.py --check: expect a line containing 1 gate error(s), and a line containing up to date; gates passed again once you revert. Then deliberately mismatch a CSS pairing, rebuild with build.py and run --check. Here it still says gates passed.
  6. Run python tools/sds_apps.py to print the colour-distance warnings and have a person look; today it lists 7 pairs under dE00 8.

Don't leave a contrast rule as a sentence in a doc. Make the build compute it from a list of colour pairs, and check that the list matches the pairs your CSS actually uses. We have only done the first half. The next step is a --check stage that extracts the text token of every rule with a bg-accent-weak background and compares it with the 11 pairs, and before that, measuring the .note body text and the .ax-cta text for the first time.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Measuring text contrast: all 3 parts

  1. Our contrast checker passed while skipping 40% of the text: make it print how much it measured

This is the last part.

FAQ

Which text does the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast minimum apply to?

Normal-size text. WCAG 2 success criterion 1.4.3 sets 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Our gate ignores text size and applies 4.5:1 to all 11 pairs.

How is a contrast ratio calculated?

Take the relative luminance of both colours, L1 for the lighter and L2 for the darker, and compute (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05). Relative luminance linearises the sRGB channels and sums 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B. The contrast() function in sds_apps.py is this formula.

Sources: the site repository's git history and its colour-token module (tools/sds_apps.py), and the design docs in our utilities app repository. Ratios were recomputed on 3 and 4 November 2026 in a copy of the site with that module's functions; the values after the 13 November refresh and the live screenshot are from that day.

item.title: Removing a feature after it moved to a sibling app – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Retrospective

10,001 lines of greeting cards: built with an AI agent, removed with one

When a feature moves to another app, delete it from the original in the same release. Our spelling app removed its greeting cards eight months late, and that release took the APK from 25.66 MB to 13.15 MB.

Reworking a long-running spelling app 7/8

With an AI coding agent, adding a feature is easy, and features nobody uses linger. SugarSpeller, our Korean spell-check app, had a greeting card feature that we built with an agent in 41 commits in the autumn of 2025. In January 2026 the code moved into a sibling app, SugarCard, yet it stayed in the original for eight more months, until one commit on September 20 deleted 143 files and 10,001 lines. Below: where the removed size really came from, what happened to users who had picked that mode, and the order we would follow next time a feature moves to a sibling app.

13.70 MB of deleted files, 0.22 MB of app Kotlin

The removal commit deleted 124 files, modified 18 and added one. The deletions covered three greeting screens (ActivityMainGreeting, a card editor and a card fragment), a Room database for cards, an MP4 encoder and audio muxer for a falling-snow video, the card images, seven carols, a handwriting font called Gamja Flower, 13 unit tests and one instrumented test. Of the 10,001 deleted lines, 7,857 were Kotlin and 2,124 were XML.

Summing the original blob sizes of the deleted files gives 13.70 MB, and the 15 app Kotlin sources account for 0.22 MB of it. The 69 files in the card image folder came to 6.68 MB, one background image, retro.png, to 3.91 MB, the font to 1.07 MB, the seven carols to 1.02 MB and the Lottie snow animation to 0.34 MB. (The commit message rounds the first three to 6.5, 3.8 and 1.1 MB.)

The sizes below come from the CHANGELOG. The baseline is the pre-change HEAD (1.6.019) rebuilt in the same environment.

1.6.019 baseline1.6.020
APK (unsigned)25.66 MB13.15 MB (−48.7%)
AAB29.95 MB18.33 MB (−38.8%)
DEX (uncompressed)16.31 MB14.84 MB (−9.0%)

Crediting that whole drop to the greeting cards would be wrong. The same release carried the commit that deleted the single -dontoptimize line that had kept R8 from optimizing. The CHANGELOG splits the result: about 11 MB was greeting card assets, and the optimization's share sits inside the 1.5 MB DEX reduction. The optimization side has its own note, Play Console said our DEX was 39% optimized.

Commits claimed 95% coverage; the repo had no coverage tool

38 of the 41 commits that built the feature credit Claude. The first commit, on August 31, 2025, added 2,495 lines across 21 files, built the card list and a Room module, and claimed "95% coverage (30+ test cases)". Two more commits that day fixed a clash between Material 3 and the app's existing theme. On September 3, a commit titled as a complete Y2K glitch-neon card editor, touched 60 files and reported "zero memory leaks and crashes". On September 10 greeting cards became a third screen mode, UIMode.GREETING, next to the chat and classic layouts. Holiday categories followed in late November, and on December 7 and 8 a ten-second falling-snow MP4 share and seven carols.

24 of the 41 commits landed in September 2025. Together they added 18,087 lines and deleted 9,188 (docs included, over 102 days).

Five of those commits (six, counting a docs commit from the same week) claim 95% or 99% test coverage. Neither git log --all -S jacoco nor -S kover returns a single line anywhere in the repository's history, so no coverage tool was ever installed. The habit of writing "complete" into commit subjects is counted in A year of AI coding in 701 commits. The Room database that the first commit called "a complete greeting module" had zero callers in the app code (main) outside its own four files when it was deleted. And on September 11, a commit made the greeting screen the default for users with no saved mode and forced that mode in debug builds. About 24 hours later the next commit put the default back to chat. The next release tag was November 28, so no shipped version had the greeting default.

A third main screen, and a copy kept for eight months

Greeting cards came in as one of three parallel main screens, not as a separate module. Card artwork and carols therefore shipped in the APK of every user who only wanted spell checks, and any fix to the main screen had to be made three times.

The structure stayed after the sibling app existed. SugarCard's first commit, on January 15, 2026, started with 297 files and 17,030 lines, and its message says "Greeting card functionality migrated from sugarspeller". Nobody removed the feature from the original app at that point. Between then and September 13, five commits in the spell-check app edited ActivityMainGreeting, and all five were shared fixes for ads or the back button made alongside the chat screen. The September 13 fix for "press back again to exit" changed 26, 23 and 22 lines in the three screens. We found no record of why the removal waited.

When a feature moves to another app, delete it from the original app in the same release. During those eight months this app got five shared fixes that also had to patch a screen that already lived in SugarCard.

Two menu entries became links; saved values fall back to chat

On the night of September 20 the operator said the feature had been forced into the app, and asked to take greeting cards out entirely, keep the two buttons in the side drawer and the top mode menu but send them to SugarCard, and focus the app on Korean spelling. The operator also expected the app to get much smaller. Six minutes later the operator added Play's code optimization requirement (deadline February 2027) to the same job, which became the R8 commit above. The removal commit landed 35 minutes after the first request.

The kept buttons now call a new SugarCardLauncher. If SugarCard is installed it opens the app; otherwise it tries market://, and if that fails, the https store page. Since Android 11 (API 30) an app has to declare another package under <queries> in its manifest to see whether it is installed, so the manifest gained one entry. Each tap logs sugarcard_open(installed) to GA4.

Users who had picked greeting mode before updating still have the string "greeting" in their settings. The code that reads the mode already sent unknown values to chat:

fun fromString(value: String?): UIMode {
    return values().find { it.value == value } ?: CHAT
}

So there is no migration code. UIModeTest gained one test asserting that "greeting" resolves to CHAT, with a comment saying these users must not get stuck behind the splash screen.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The agent guessed 10 MB and 9 tests; a person checked the device

The agent's plan named the screens and modules to remove, but its numbers were low. It added card images (6.5 MB), retro.png (3.8 MB) and the snow animation (0.3 MB) to get "roughly 10 MB", and counted 9 unit tests to delete. The real commit also removed the font and the seven carols, and deleted 13 unit tests.

The agent had no device attached, said so, and left a release APK signed with the debug key. It asked the operator to try checks against Naver and Daum (two Korean portals whose spell-check results the app parses), history, subscriptions, KakaoTalk sharing and the greeting card menu. The operator replied the next day that everything worked, and 1.6.020 shipped on September 22.

One wrong assumption stayed in the launcher. If opening market:// threw, it fell back to the browser, and the comment on that branch read "device without the Play Store app". On October 9 the same pattern was added for a games menu. On a Galaxy S21 the link showed a chooser instead of an exception, because three store apps accepted it. A commit 59 minutes after the games commit made both the game and SugarCard links target the Play package first. The full account is in A market:// link opens a store chooser on SKT-sold Samsung phones.

The menus stayed, opened the app first, and shipped in one release

Deleting the menus too was ruled out by the operator's first request. The Korean label lost its "switch to" wording, since tapping it no longer switches modes.

Sending every tap straight to the store was an option the agent raised in its plan. The operator kept the app-first order, which is why the manifest needs <queries>. As the launcher comment says, without that declaration the installed check always fails and every tap goes to the store.

Shipping the removal and the R8 change in separate releases would have made the size change easy to attribute. The operator chose to ship them together, which is why the size section uses a separately built baseline.

Stored user data would change the order

This removal needed no data migration only because no screen called the Room database by the time of removal (none had since September 3, 2025, and no release shipped while one did). If users had saved cards in it, an export path or a handoff to the sibling app would have to come first.

If the mode parser had thrown on unknown values, one test would not have been enough. Updated users could get stuck at launch, and a migration that rewrites the saved value would have to ship first.

We found no record of how often the greeting screens were used; the only numbers are menu taps after the removal. For a feature many people use, check screen usage before deleting it.

Steps for handing a feature to a sibling app

  1. Count the files and bytes to be deleted with git. Get the deleted blobs from git diff --raw and sum them with git cat-file -s, so you know whether lines or bytes dominate.
  2. Count the callers of the module with git grep -l. Zero callers outside the module means no data migration.
  3. Read where a saved setting goes when its value no longer exists, and pin that path with one unit test.
  4. If the menu stays, add a sibling-app launcher. Declare the package under <queries>, and open the store in this order: market:// targeted at the Play package, plain market://, then the https page.
  5. Compare sizes against the pre-change HEAD built in the same environment. If the release has other changes, split the shares.
  6. Install the release APK on a real device and tap the kept menu with the sibling app installed and not installed.
  7. Log menu taps with the installed state to see demand.

We don't yet know whether the 54 taps became installs

In the two weeks after release (September 22 to October 5), sugarcard_open fired 54 times from about 39 users, and SugarCard was installed at the moment of the tap in none of them, so every tap went to the store (GA4, per the monitoring document). Another 61 SugarCard taps came in from October 9 to 22; installed only records the state at tap time. Starting with 1.6.027 the event is called sibling_app_open (target=sugarcard); the next step is to line it up against SugarCard's install sources.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Reworking a long-running spelling app: all 8 parts

  1. A 20% staged rollout went out at 100%: a completed release in the Play Publisher API cannot go back to staged
  2. Quiz reach rose from 2.6% to 17.7%, and 63% of quiz opens came from one morning notification

FAQ

What happens to users who saved a mode that the update removes?

It depends on where the parser sends unknown values. This app's fromString already mapped unknown values to chat, so a leftover "greeting" opens the chat screen, and a unit test pins that path.

I removed a feature and the APK barely shrank. What should I check?

Check the bytes of the deleted files first. Here 10,001 lines went away but the app's Kotlin sources were 0.22 MB; the size came from images, a font and audio.

Why does my check for another installed app always say "not installed"?

Since Android 11 (API 30), getLaunchIntentForPackage only finds the other app if its package is declared under <queries> in the manifest. The removal commit declared just SugarCard's package; more were added later for the games menu.

Sources: git history of the spell-check app and of SugarCard, the spell-check app's CHANGELOG entry for 1.6.020, a post-release monitoring document (GA4 counts), and the work session log of September 20 to 22, 2026. Numbers were recounted from git on November 4, 2026.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Jetpack Compose splits Korean between syllables, but the stacked 'R/u/l/e' label came from how a Row measures
  • Three agent designs, three judges: the market judge alone would have picked the one that crashed on every KakaoTalk file
