item.title: SAF PDF save: cancelling without empty files – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · How-to

We pressed BACK at seven moments before shipping one 'Save as PDF' button

BACK pressed at seven delays after the Save tap split cancel from done at 0.9 to 1.0 s on a Galaxy S20 and 0.75 to 0.9 s on a Galaxy S21, and left no empty file.

Building the SugarDoc HWP viewer 5/8

When an Android app saves a PDF through the system file picker (the Storage Access Framework, SAF), an empty file exists the moment the user taps Save. Press BACK right after, and you can be left with an empty or half-written file. On October 18, 2026 we checked 'Save as PDF' in HWP Viewer SugarDoc 1.2.0 on a minified release build, pressing BACK at seven moments between 0.3 and 1.8 s after the Save tap. Neither side of either boundary left a partial file, and only then did 'PDF Save' go into the store title.

The BACK boundary: 0.9 to 1.0 s on the S20, 0.75 to 0.9 s on the S21

The test document was a 47-page HWP file (HWP is the Korean word processor format the app opens). SugarDoc saves at most the first 15 pages of a long document, so the save shows a notice that only the first 15 of 47 pages will be saved and then writes a 15-page PDF. After tapping Save in the system file picker, the script sent BACK at 0.3, 0.45, 0.6, 0.75, 0.9, 1.0 and 1.8 s, then checked the Download folder: was a file left, and if so, did it start with %PDF-, end with %%EOF and hold all 15 pages?

On the Galaxy S20 (Android 13), BACK up to 0.9 s cancelled the save and the file was deleted; from 1.0 s the save had already finished and the full 15-page PDF stayed. On the Galaxy S21 (Android 15), BACK cancelled up to 0.75 s and met a finished save from 0.9 s. Neither phone produced a zero-byte file, a header-only file or a crash.

Three conditions before 'PDF Save' could go in the title

SugarDoc had a 'Print / Save as PDF' menu item since 1.0.0: it opened the system print screen, where the user picks 'Save as PDF' instead of a printer. On October 17 we started work on the app's Play search ranking, and the lead agent assumed PDF saving had never shipped. A research agent that read the code corrected it. What was missing was a direct save that skips the print screen, and a store title that says the app can do it.

The ASO plan written that day put three conditions on the new title, 'SugarDoc HWP Viewer & PDF Save' in English: the direct save ships; a minified release build saves and reopens a PDF on recorded devices; the saved PDF opens in another PDF app. A user who arrives from that title and meets a print dialog is likely to leave a one-star "PDF save doesn't work" review, and with zero reviews at the time, that one review would be the whole rating.

Two ways of building it were dropped. Drawing pages into a PdfDocument inside the app had already failed an earlier spike: a 50-page manual peaked at 1.95 GB of memory and writeTo took 10.9 s, and bundling fonts would push the APK past its 26 MB size gate. Saving past the 15-page cap by writing 15-page chunks and merging them was out too: the WebView renderer holds about 7 to 8 MB per page until the document closes, and a PDF merge library would need its own license check. So the save keeps the WebView PrintDocumentAdapter the print path already used and only swaps the destination for a document SAF creates. The cap stays the same as printing: 15 pages, 6 on low-end phones.

One save passes five stages, and the empty file comes first

'Save as PDF' starts the system picker with ActivityResultContracts.CreateDocument("application/pdf"), which is SAF's ACTION_CREATE_DOCUMENT. When the user names the file and taps Save, the document provider creates an empty document right there and returns its URI. The app records that URI as a just-picked target and refuses to write or delete any URI that is not on that list, because the app has a rule never to write to a user's original files.

Next the app lays out the pages through the same path as printing, opens the file on an IO thread with openFileDescriptor(uri, "wt") (falling back to "w" for providers that refuse truncation), and calls onStart, onLayout, onWrite and onFinish on the WebView print adapter itself, with no print dialog. The result callbacks have constructors that are package-private in the SDK, so only that piece lives in the android.print package, as a 99-line file; there is no reflection. When the write ends the app checks for a zero-byte file and closes it. A failed or cancelled save deletes the created document with DocumentsContract.deleteDocument.

The document exists before any byte is written, so a stop at any later stage leaves a named, empty PDF in the user's folder unless the app deletes it. Close and delete is the default on any stop, but while the WebView is writing to the fd, closing it was the dangerous part.

Defect 1: the fd was closed while the WebView was still writing

The implementing agent's first version closed the fd and deleted the file as soon as a save stopped, whether from BACK, a timeout or the reader closing, without waiting for the WebView's write result. Its report listed this as a risk and assumed that a late write would simply fail. The debug build passed 17/17 on both phones and all 504 unit tests were green.

A review agent started in a fresh context rated that assumption a High defect. According to the review and the code comment that now sits on the writer, the WebView (Chromium's AwPrintManager) writes to the raw fd number from a background thread without duplicating it. Once the app closes the number, another file the app opens next, a database or a document copy, can get the same number, and the late PDF bytes land in that file instead of failing. onFinish was also being called before the write ended. We did not open the Chromium source ourselves this time.

The fixed writer reports a settled flag with the result. A stop before the write starts is settled, so the app closes and deletes at once. A stop during the write is not settled: the app leaves the fd open, never counts it as saved and deletes the document, and the writer calls onFinish and closes the fd after the adapter's own write result arrives. If the WebView never answers, one fd stays open until the process ends; the review judged that a smaller harm than a corrupted file. Three Robolectric tests pin this rule.

No person edited this code. The review happened because of the operator's standing rules: get a review from a separate context after a large change, and do not call anything done before the minified release build has run on real phones.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Defects 2 and 3 sat in the short gap while the file opened

Defect 2 lost BACK presses. The cancel handle was registered when the write started, and while the file was opening on the IO thread after page layout, the handle was still empty, so a BACK in that gap was ignored and the save went on. The implementing agent had listed this gap among its risks. The review added a pending-cancel flag that stops the write the moment the handle is registered, plus one controller test.

Defect 3 was the Activity going away while the file opened. If the coroutine was cancelled there, the opened result could be dropped: the fd would leak, an empty PDF could stay in the user's folder and the progress cover could stay up. Now the cancellation handler closes the fd, deletes the document, ends the save as cancelled and rethrows. This is Activity code, so there is no JVM test; it was checked on the phones by recreating the screen and killing the process.

After the three fixes, unit tests stood at 508 debug (504 + 3 + 1) and 469 release, all passing. The guard-removal table, which deletes each guard in turn and expects a test to fail, grew from 29 to 32 rows. The review also noted that some existing rows only pinned source strings, so breaking the behaviour while keeping the string would still pass; the Robolectric tests cover that. The guard-removal method has its own note, Catch fake AI-written tests by deleting their guards.

Four of the first five delays hit a finished save

The release-checking agent first chose BACK delays of 0.3, 1.0, 1.8, 2.6 and 3.5 s. In the first S21 run, on an earlier build with the flag on, only 0.3 s cancelled. The other four all left a complete 15-page PDF of 851,990 bytes: BACK arrived after the save had finished and just closed the reader, leaving the launcher on top.

Seeing that, the agent packed six delays between 0.3 and 1.0 s and kept 1.8 s, which produced the boundaries at the top of this note. The same first run had two failures, both from the test method. The developer option always_finish_activities did not take effect when changed at run time, so Activity recreation moved to a font_scale change and process death to am kill. Chrome 155 on the phones would not open a content:// PDF, so the Chrome check stopped counting as pass or fail.

On the 1.2.0 (5) build the 37 items passed 37/37 on the S21 and 36/37 on the S20. The S20 failure came from uiautomator dump dying with an NPE. The base script's crash filter did not match on the package name, so it counted the test tool's crash; that log had zero lines from the app's package. A rerun on the earlier flag-on build scored 37/37 on both phones.

The SAF save checklist we ran on the release build

These are the items from the 37 that carry over to other apps, in order. Run all of them on a minified release build with the feature flag on; a debug build never exercises code that R8 removed or rewrote.

  1. Cancel in the picker and confirm no file appears.
  2. Save a small document and check the %PDF- header, %%EOF and the page count. We used a 3-page HWPX.
  3. Save a document over the cap and check the notice and the capped page count (15).
  4. Reopen the saved PDF in the app twice. We got 15 drawn pages and 0 failed pages.
  5. Find when the save finishes with a coarse grid of BACK delays, then press again every 0.15 s in front of that point. Each time, check for leftover files, zero bytes, header and end marker, and crashes.
  6. Cancel with BACK after 0.15 s, then save again and confirm it works.
  7. Recreate the Activity while the picker is up, and 0, 0.3 and 0.6 s after the save. Changing font_scale does it.
  8. Kill the process with am kill while the picker is up and confirm no empty file is left when the result comes back.
  9. Count Accessing hidden lines for the app process, StrictMode and R8 errors (ClassNotFound, NoSuchMethod) in logcat, and filter the crash buffer by the app's package. All were 0 on this build.
  10. Open the saved PDF in another PDF app. The phone's Chrome refused it, so we checked all 15 pages in desktop Chrome.

If you ship a SAF save, do not stop after pressing BACK at one moment. Here cancel and done were 0.1 to 0.15 s apart. On Oct 18, the day of this run, the operator ran the production promotion by hand around noon, and the new title went in a few minutes later.

Whether BACK hit the write stage could not be seen from outside

From outside the phone there was no way to tell whether BACK landed during page layout or while the bytes were being written to the file. What we know is that on both sides of the cancel-to-done boundary (0.75 to 1.0 s) there were no leftover files, no zero-byte files and no crashes. We did not watch the defect 1 fix act mid-write on a device.

The boundaries come from two phones and one 47-page document. Another phone or another document will have its own boundary, so the grid has to be found again. The write-timeout path cannot be forced on a device and was checked only by unit tests. If a document provider hands over a pipe instead of a regular file, the size reads as -1, the zero-byte check does nothing, and the app trusts the adapter's result callback alone.

The WebView print path and the 222-document measurements are in Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents.

A 6-page-cap phone and saving to Drive are still untested

We had no phone in the low-end tier (6-page cap), so that path has only unit tests. Saves went only to the default Download folder; Google Drive, SD cards and other document providers were not tried. There are no records yet for an S23, tablets or foldables, landscape, or saving with TalkBack on. For Drive, the first question is whether it actually takes the pipe path above.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Building the SugarDoc HWP viewer: all 8 parts

  1. androidx.pdf beta01 runs your Application.onCreate a second time, in an isolated process, and the PDF silently never opens
  2. We built an edit feature and shipped it switched off: the HWP save gate that caught a form-field bug

FAQ

Does cancelling ACTION_CREATE_DOCUMENT leave an empty file?

Cancelling in the picker returns a null URI and creates no file. After the user taps Save, the provider creates an empty document first, so if your write fails or is cancelled after that, you must delete it yourself with DocumentsContract.deleteDocument.

Can I close the ParcelFileDescriptor right away when the user cancels?

Only if the write has not started. If a WebView print adapter is already writing, keep the fd open until the adapter's write result arrives. Another file of your app can reuse a number you closed early, and late PDF bytes can land in it.

Can a WebView be saved as a PDF without the print dialog?

It can: call onStart, onLayout, onWrite and onFinish on the adapter from createPrintDocumentAdapter yourself. The result callback constructors are package-private in the SDK, so the file that creates them must sit in the android.print package, and you should check a release build for hidden-API warnings and R8 errors.

Sources: the SugarDoc 1.2.0 release record and the October 18 commits, the store listing plan, and agent reports from October 17-18 (rechecked November 4). Device serials are left out.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Claude Code Android: a build gate for zero ads
  • Commits without a Co-Authored-By trailer: the agent made 26 of the 29 we could check

item.title: Gemini in an Android app: cost, eval, daily caps – SugarMount
item.description:
AX Notes · Measurement

The first LLM feature in a spell-check app: cost, model evaluation and daily caps for "Why is this wrong?"

Adding an LLM to an app means choosing a model, a billing path and a spending cap. Our spelling app picked its model with a 59-case eval, and its server function stops calling the LLM after 3,000 calls a day.

Adding an LLM to an app 1/4

The first eval run on the night of September 27, 2026 failed on all 59 calls with HTTP 402. It used an AI Studio key that the coding agent had said around noon that day would be billed against our Firebase credit, and we were in the middle of giving our Korean spelling app SugarSpeller its first server function and LLM. After the key was replaced with Vertex AI, gemini-3.8-flash gave a correct reason for all 59 corrections (the right rule for 54), with a p95 latency of 4.3 seconds and a cost of $0.93 per 1,000 calls. In the two weeks after the October 1 release, 3.7% of users who ran a check tapped the button; among users who had opened the correction sheet, it was 41%.

Sources: the design doc in the app repository (approved 2026-09-27), git history, the release decision log and the work log. Usage is from GA4; cost is from the usage records the function writes (checked 2026-11-02, times in UTC+9).

The 59-case eval: flash-lite at 78%, 3.8-flash at 100%

The feature explains one correction at a time: the user taps a corrected word and gets a one-line reason plus the name of the Korean orthography rule behind it. We picked the model with 59 corrections taken from real checker responses stored as test fixtures in the app: 38 from Naver's spell checker and 21 from Daum's (Naver and Daum are the two big Korean portals, and the app uses their checkers). The pass mark was written into the design doc before the run: at least 90% correct and a p95 of 2.5 seconds or less. Every call went to the Vertex AI global endpoint.

Model (prompt)Reason correctRule also correctp50 / p95Per 1,000
gemini-3.5-flash-lite (v1)43/59 (73%)30/591.06 s / 1.26 s$0.27
gemini-3.5-flash-lite (v2)46/59 (78%)38/591.08 s / 4.6 s$0.42
gemini-3.8-flash (v2)59/59 (100%)54/59 (92%)2.0 s / 4.3 s$0.93

Prompt v2 added an order of checks for spacing errors and a table of reasons for the most common corrections. It moved flash-lite from 73% to 78% and no further. Its wrong answers included explaining a noun fused with hada ("to do") as an ending or particle, garbled syllables, and calling an archaic spelling of a polite ending a past tense. 3.8-flash made no typos; its five misses were all wrong rule citations. It costs more than twice as much as flash-lite v2 per 1,000 calls, and it was the only model over the 90% bar, so it became the default.

The first 3.8-flash run returned 59 empty answers. The model's thinking tokens used up the 160-token output limit before any JSON came out; setting thinkingBudget: 0 fixed it. The 2.5-second target was missed. This model is served only from the global endpoint (the Seoul and Tokyo regions returned 404), and each call took 2.1 to 2.8 seconds. Because that was still inside the app's 8-second timeout and the button shows a progress indicator, the design doc moved the target to a p95 of 5 seconds.

The AI Studio key never touched the $300 credit

The 402 came from billing. The error read Your prepayment credits are depleted, and authentication had succeeded. In this project, AI Studio billing was prepaid only, so it had no link to the 90-day $300 free-trial credit (held in Cloud Billing) that came with moving the Firebase project to the pay-as-you-go Blaze plan.

At 12:01 the agent wrote that with the $300 credit, paid-tier Gemini API usage would be billed to the same project, and ten minutes later it produced a table showing the credit applied to both. The spec switched to keyless Vertex AI at 12:18, then at 12:21 went back to an AI Studio key the operator had already created, on the grounds that it shared the billing account.

The function, the quota code and the cache were all tested against a fake provider during the day, so the first real Gemini call was the eval run around 10 p.m. When the agent reported the 402 at 22:04, its first recommendation was to buy AI Studio prepaid credit (minimum $5). At 22:06 the operator asked why, if the $300 was supposed to cover it. The agent then said its earlier explanation was wrong: AI Studio keys used to bill a project's Cloud billing account after the fact, and this project didn't work that way.

A commit at 22:10 moved Gemini authentication to Vertex AI with ADC (Application Default Credentials, the service account the code already runs as). Vertex bills through Cloud Billing, which per the design doc is where the credit applies, and there is no API key to store or rotate. The deploy 49 minutes later hit one more snag: declaring an unused secret on the function was enough to make the deploy query Secret Manager and fail with 403, so the secret is now declared only in key mode.

Before building an LLM feature, make one real call and check which bill it lands on. A 200 response does not say which balance paid for it. After the move to Vertex, this app computed its cost from token counts the function records times the list price, and the repository has no record of the credit deduction being checked against a billing report.

The function refuses LLM calls past 3,000 a day

explainCorrection is a single callable function on Cloud Functions for Firebase (2nd gen). The app signs in anonymously when its process opens the first screen, and the Firebase SDK attaches the auth token to each call. The function validates input, checks the cache, takes from the quota, calls the LLM, then stores the result. The cache comes before the quota, so an explanation that already exists costs the user nothing.

ControlDefaultHow to change it
Free quota5 a day per anonymous uidFirestore doc config/limits (cached 60 s)
Subscriber ceiling100 a day per uidSame doc
Global cap3,000 LLM attempts a daySame doc; 0 closes it
App Check enforcementOff (measured only); current setting unconfirmedrequireAppCheck in the same doc
Button in the appOnRemote Config explain_enabled = false

The day rolls over at midnight Korea time. The day key is computed by adding nine hours to UTC milliseconds rather than trusting the server's time zone. The global cap counts LLM attempts, not requests: retries and hedged duplicates each count, and only attempts that failed before billing (network errors and the like) are given back. Timeouts stay counted, because the provider may already have charged for them.

A budget alert sends an email and does not stop charges, which is why the design doc calls the 3,000-call cap the real safeguard. At the eval price ($0.93), a full day at the cap is about $2.8; with the longer v3 prompt from September 28 (about $1.1 per 1,000) it is about $3.3 by our calculation. A call cap works as a money cap only because each call is bounded: the original and corrected words are limited to 60 code points each, and the output to 160 tokens. The agent's morning estimate (under 0.1 won per call, under 1,000 won a month) used flash-lite prices; the chosen model costs 3.4 times flash-lite v1 per 1,000 calls.

In the first release stage the function trusts the app's claim that the user subscribes. A forged claim buys 95 extra explanations a day at under 10 won (well under a cent), so receipt checks were deferred. Putting the daily total document in the same transaction as the user's quota made concurrent requests die on lock timeouts, and on September 28 the total moved outside the transaction. As a result, the global cap can overshoot by the number of requests in flight.

Remote Config refreshed only on the launcher screen, and people who used only the mini window (opened from text selection in another app) never pass through it, so switching off explain_enabled would have left their button in place. The September 29 release review caught it, and the mini window now fetches config before it opens the sheet.

A 7.9-second cold start pushed the app timeout to 15 seconds

The smoke test after the production deploy on the night of September 27 measured 7.9 seconds for the first call and 1.6 to 3.0 seconds after that. The function runs with zero minimum instances, and the app's timeout was 8 seconds, so a cold call came within 0.1 seconds of it. So the app timeout went up to 15 seconds. Keeping one instance warm (about $3 to $4 a month) stayed in the function docs as a fallback if cold starts became a problem. LLM calls on October 26 and 27 cost $0.020 in total, so the warm instance would cost far more than the feature itself.

The next day, one repeated eval call that stretched to 44.5 seconds set the server-side deadlines: 6 seconds per attempt and 12 for the whole request. From October 25 the function hedges: if an attempt is silent for 4 seconds, it sends the same request again and takes whichever answers first. Failures went from 16 of 25 in the October 24 function log to 0 of 16 on October 26 and 27.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

3.7% of checking users, 41% of sheet openers

The decision rule went into the decision log before release. Fourteen days in, if 8% or more of users who ran a check tapped the button, keep it; under 3%, test a new position and wording. The October 17 review (October 2 to 16, app 1.6.025 or later) counted 56 of 1,527 checking users, 3.7%, with 77 requests. That sits between the two thresholds.

Over the same period, 138 users (9.0%) tapped a corrected word to open the sheet, and 56 of them pressed the button. 41% of people who reached the sheet wanted the reason, so the bottleneck was finding the sheet rather than the button. Version 1.6.031, rolled out in stages from October 18, added a one-time hint that the highlighted words can be tapped.

With about 8 requests a day, the 14-day cache hit rate was 11% against a 40% target. How the shared cache key was built is covered in the blind A/B that let us stop sending context to the LLM.

Mass-created anonymous accounts hit only the global cap

A uid's quota starts over when the app is reinstalled. A script that keeps creating anonymous accounts makes the per-user limit of 5 meaningless; what remains is the global 3,000 and App Check, which defaults to measuring only. If one explanation were expensive, verify the subscription on the server from day one.

The 59 cases came only from the checkers' red, green and blue groups (Naver red 25, green 13; Daum red 14, green 5, blue 2); there was not one purple or violet case, and the September 27 scoring was done by the same agent that wrote the code. No human scored it. A model that lives only on the global endpoint also changes what a privacy policy can say about where data is processed; another of our apps ran into that with the same model, written up in the privacy-policy note on AI processing location.

Adding the same feature to your app

  1. Make one real model call through a path that bills to Cloud Billing (Vertex AI here). On 402 or 403, stop and settle the billing path first. On 200, check the billing report for the credit deduction.
  2. Pull about 50 cases from your app's test data and put accuracy, p95 and cost per 1,000 calls for each candidate in one table. Write the pass mark first, and set the thinking budget of thinking models to 0.
  3. Expose one callable function that requires anonymous auth, with three limits (free per user, subscriber ceiling, global) keyed by day in your users' time zone. Keep the limits in a document you can change without a deploy, with 0 meaning closed.
  4. Cap input length and output tokens.
  5. Give the app a remote switch that hides the button, and check that every entry screen refreshes it.
  6. After the production deploy, time the first call to a cold instance and set the app timeout above it. Before release, write the decision rule: two usage thresholds, cache hit rate, failure rate and daily cost.

The default limits and the thinking switch (MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS is 160):

// default limits
export const DEFAULT_LIMITS: Limits = { freePerDay: 5, entitledPerDay: 100, globalPerDay: 3000, requireAppCheck: false };
// Gemini generateContent config, in part
maxOutputTokens: MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS,
thinkingConfig: { thinkingBudget: 0 },

Still open: usage after the tap hint, and a price doubling

The tap hint in 1.6.031 is judged by whether 6% or more of users who saw it request an explanation. The review was due November 1, and as of November 2 the log has no row for it yet. 3.8-flash is scheduled to double in price on January 1, 2027, to $1.50 input and $7.50 output per million tokens; on that day the prices and the worst-day figure need recalculating. We also haven't seen a real bill yet, since the 90-day credit is still running.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Adding an LLM to an app: all 4 parts

  1. A shared LLM cache could have frozen a prompt injection: the blind A/B that let us stop sending context

FAQ

Can Firebase Blaze credit pay for the Gemini API?

Per the design doc, only Vertex AI is on the credit path in this project; we haven't confirmed it on an invoice yet. The AI Studio key was on prepaid-only billing, so all 59 eval calls on September 27, 2026 were rejected with 402.

How do you cap the cost of an LLM feature?

Count LLM calls inside the function and refuse them past a daily limit. A budget alert only sends an email. This app closes at 3,000 calls a day, and one Firestore document can change that number or set it to 0 without a deploy.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • We slowed a mini game down twice before checking why it was hard: players couldn't recall the answers
  • Claude Code scheduled runs: state left behind

All AX notes

item.title: Guarding a game result card against rapid taps – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

Rapid taps and an unlocked Retry button: a 600 ms result-card lock, and the 28 crashes a stress run found next

Keep result-card buttons from accepting taps for a short while after they appear (600 ms in this game). If a burst of taps runs on, the next tap can restart the level before the player has seen the result.

If a result card appears while the player is still hammering the screen, a leftover tap can hit the card's Retry button and restart the level before the player has even seen the result. On October 2, 2026 we reproduced an operator report ("I still had hearts and it suddenly started over") from Arrow Knots, our then-unreleased puzzle game, on a Galaxy S21: eight taps on a blocked arrow, 70 ms apart, drained all three hearts in under 250 ms, and the loss card that followed had a Retry button that took taps the instant it showed.

After locking the card buttons for 600 ms, the operator asked for a stress run that plays all 300 levels back to back. Its first pass crashed the app 28 times; the cause was a spring animation overshooting until an index in the drawing code hit -1. Below: how both defects were reproduced and fixed, and how to check another game for the same things.

Three hearts gone within 250 ms, and no lock on the card's button

In Arrow Knots you tap an arrow and it slides out head first. If something is in the way, it pokes forward, bounces back, and you lose a heart. On level 50 the navy arrow in the top-left corner was blocked by a purple arrow near the top right. The agent tapped that arrow over adb:

adb shell 'for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do input tap 360 534 & sleep 0.07; done; wait'

Every tap on that arrow during the bounce back counted as a new mistake. The device log shows three blocked taps within 160 ms; the other five taps arrived after game over. Per the session report, the heart display jumped to the final count in a contact callback, so the hearts were still on screen at the moment the last one was lost. On a loss the code waits 550 ms and shows the loss card, and the card's button had no input lock. In this run the last tap (08:37:11.427) came before the card appeared, and the log shows no restart.

The operator's own guess in the report, that it seemed to happen on mistakes, pointed the right way. The commit message names this path as the cause: the next tap lands on the loss card's Retry button and restarts the level unseen.

The operator's symptom could also be explained by the crash found later. That crash also came from tapping a blocked arrow, which is a mistake, and reopening the app after it starts the level over. A crash can restart the level even with hearts left; a restart through the card means the hearts were already at zero and only the display lagged. What this session reproduced on the device was the crash itself, and we read the card path as a possibility that follows from the button's missing lock in the code. With no log from the operator's S24 we could not tell which one it was, and the two fixes below closed both paths.

Ignore the bouncing arrow, drop hearts one at a time, lock the card for 600 ms

The first fix made four changes:

  • A repeat tap on an arrow that is still bouncing back is dropped. The check is fx.isBumping(id) && !state.canRemove(id); every other arrow stays tappable.
  • The heart display drops one heart per contact (lives = maxOf(state.lives, lives - 1)).
  • The result card's button ignores taps for 600 ms after it appears: a RESULT_ARM_MS = 600L constant, a LaunchedEffect that waits that long, then clickable(enabled = armed).
  • When a bounce finishes, it no longer clears animations that an exit has started on the same arrow in the meantime.

The same eight-tap burst now cost two hearts instead of three; the eighth tap arrived after the arrow was home and counted as a new mistake. Hammering the button area right after the loss card appeared left the card in place, and a tap after 600 ms restarted the level as it should.

The agent guessed the "crash" was a misreading. The app could crash after all

The report had a second symptom: tap the top-left of level 50 quickly and the app closes. On the build before the fix, the agent mixed rapid taps on that arrow, the pause button and the Retry button for 30 seconds, and ran three fresh-install monkey runs on the fixed build. No crash showed up in the log. In its 08:49 report the agent wrote that the operator may have taken the sudden restart for a crash, and asked for the operator's Galaxy S24 to be plugged in over USB if the app had really closed.

The operator had the fix committed, then asked for a hard stress test, coordinated with the other session so nothing was left broken. The crash came out of the suite built for that request. Don't close an unreproduced crash as "the user probably misread it." Run a test that plays the game for well over an hour on the same device first (85 minutes for the first pass here, 99 for the rerun).

First stress run: 5,091 seconds, 30 failures

The agent started with an engine fuzz test: 20 random games on each of the 300 levels, about 1.8 million taps through the rules engine, with zero rule violations, exceptions or dead ends. Then a stress script ran on the S21 in four phases:

  • campaign: all 300 levels back to back in one process. Removable arrows are tapped in fast batches, deliberate mistakes are mixed in (keeping one heart), and about 6% of levels are lost on purpose, then Retry is tapped as the card appears.
  • burst: on 25 levels, 30 near-simultaneous taps anywhere on screen.
  • lifecycle: on 12 levels, home during an animation, pause-button spam, the back key, and process death in the background followed by a restore.
  • monkey: 12 runs of 3,000 events with pinch, back and app switches.

Each level checks logcat for FATAL EXCEPTION and ANRs and checks that the process is alive with pidof (a foreground check was added after the first pass, because of level 37). The first pass took 5,091 seconds and reported 30 failures. Twenty-eight were what the script judged a crash or ANR, the first on level 80 and the last on level 298. Cumulative failures were 1 by level 50, 5 by level 100, 11 by level 200 and 30 by level 300. The other two were not app bugs: on level 37 the app went to the background without any crash record (we took it as something outside sending it home), and on level 84 uiautomator could not read the Next button while confetti was animating.

The crash buffer had already been cleared, so the top of the first stack trace was gone and only the draw path was left. That means we could not confirm directly that all 28 were the same exception; we treat them as one cause because the rerun after the fix had zero crashes.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

A spring overshot and the draw code read points[-1]

The agent's next guess was memory. Twenty-five levels from level 76 in a fresh process passed with no failure, and the first pass had only crashed after long play.

The 10:28 note gives one clue, that the crashes clustered in the later levels with larger boards (200 and up); the surviving stack was also only the draw path. The agent suspected board size over a leak, guessed that a spring overshoot pushed the index in Track.body() out of range, and at 10:38 tapped an arrow with a far blocker. Memory was checked along the way: a rerun logging memory showed GPU memory moving between 180 and 240 MB rather than climbing.

Arrow 6 on level 22 sits 8.55 cells from the arrow that blocks it. One tap closed the app:

java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException: Index -1 out of bounds for length 23

A blocked arrow pokes forward all the way to its blocker, so a longer gap means a longer poke. It springs home with spring(dampingRatio = 0.5f, stiffness = 600f), which, per the commit message, overshoots behind the start by about 16% of the poke. The commit message puts the line at "a blocker 6+ cells away," and the TrackTest comment notes an arrow with its blocker 8.55 cells away springing back to travel of about -1.4; per the session log, that is arrow 6 on level 22. Below -1, Track.body(t), which builds the arrow's body polyline, uses floor(t) + 1 as an index and reads points[-1]. That code runs inside draw, so one exception takes the whole app down.

Level 50 has no such arrow at the start, which is why 30 seconds of scripted adb tapping found nothing. Gaps grow as the board clears, so any level could hit it mid-game, and the larger boards in later levels hit it more often.

The second fix bounds the spring with anim.updateBounds(lowerBound = -0.12f) and, if the bound is hit (AnimationEndReason.BoundReached), finishes the trip home with a 120 ms tween. Track.body clamps its index with coerceAtLeast(0) and k < points.size, so no travel value can crash it. The regression test TrackTest draws every arrow in the level pack from travel -40 to 40 past the exit in steps of 0.37, and the agent first confirmed that it fails against the old Track.kt. Three taps on each of four far-blocked arrows (levels 22, 72, 92 and 122) no longer crashed, and the full rerun (300-level campaign plus burst, lifecycle and 12 monkey runs) took 5,935 seconds with zero failures, with the fresh-install monkey check at 3/3.

We blocked one arrow, not the whole board

Locking all board input for a moment would also have stopped the tap problem. The first fix only drops repeat taps on the arrow that is bouncing. The commit just before it added a combo that rewards removing arrows in quick succession, and we think a global lock on a combo board would block legitimate fast play too; the record doesn't say why it wasn't used. Locking only the result card was another option, but hearts would still drain within 250 ms and the player would land on a loss card without knowing why. So the tap guard, the one-heart-per-contact display and the card lock shipped together.

On the crash side, making the draw code safe would have been enough to stop the app dying. The spring bound went in as well because of a reason in the code comment: the overshoot drags the arrow's tail cells behind its start, so the drawing goes wrong even without a crash.

1.8 million fuzz taps never touched the draw code

The engine fuzz test passed on the same day the app crashed 28 times. The rules engine only tracks rule state (blocking, removal, hearts); it never sees animation travel or drawing indexes.

The stress script assumes a debug build. It writes the level into the progress file with run-as and computes tap positions from board bounds printed in a debug log. As of the fix the suite had never run on an R8-minified release build, and only one device, the S21, had run it.

From an eight-tap burst to a 300-level run in six steps

  1. Pick an object that bounces when blocked and send the eight-tap burst above, 70 ms apart. Check that hearts lost match mistakes made, and that a person can actually see the result screen.
  2. Count repeat taps on an animating object as one mistake. Keep a per-object "bouncing" set, and let a tap through once the object can actually leave.
  3. Ignore the result card's buttons and the back key for a fixed time after it appears (600 ms here). Use the same constant for every button that changes the level, such as next and retry.
  4. Find draw code that turns an animation value into an array index and make it safe for any value. Bound springs with updateBounds and finish with a tween on BoundReached.
  5. Write a unit test that draws every shipped object at out-of-range values, and confirm it fails with the fix reverted.
  6. Play every level back to back in one process, mixing deliberate mistakes, deliberate losses with a Retry tap as the card appears, simultaneous taps, lifecycle events and monkey. Judge on three signals (crash or ANR in the log, the process alive, the app in the foreground) and write the full trace to a file as soon as a crash is seen. Our script checks these three after each level (replace the package name with your app's):
adb logcat -d | grep -E "FATAL EXCEPTION|ANR in your.package"
adb shell pidof your.package
adb shell "dumpsys window | grep mCurrentFocus"

The tutorial crash that the fresh-install monkey caught the night before is written up in VIBRATE crash and the fresh-install monkey test.

Next on an R8 release build: the level-22 tap and the eight-tap burst

Next is one tap on arrow 6 of level 22 and the eight-tap burst on level 50, on an R8 release build. Nothing in the record says how 600 ms was chosen, so timing card-to-first-tap in real play recordings and revisiting the value is still open.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

How do I stop rapid taps from hitting a button that just appeared in Compose?

This game uses clickable(enabled = armed) plus one state that a LaunchedEffect turns on 600 ms after the screen appears. A typical debounce, which takes the first tap and drops the rest, still accepts a first tap carried over from the previous screen, so the lock is timed from when the screen appeared.

Why didn't the monkey test find it?

The fresh-install monkey starts in the tutorial and the first levels. The defect needs a tap on an arrow whose blocker is 6 or more cells away, like arrow 6 on level 22 at 8.55 cells, and it first appeared on level 80 of a run that cleared all 300 levels.

From the October 2 record: two commits in the game repository (08:50 and 12:23 Korea time) and the agent session log between them (device logs and stress-run output).

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • We slowed a mini game down twice before checking why it was hard: players couldn't recall the answers
  • Mobile game feel: frame timing showed our heart penalty landing 109 ms before the collision
  • Block puzzle difficulty: how simulation bots caught a game you could never lose
  • A reverse-construction generator and the gate behind 1,100 arrow-puzzle levels
  • Play Store title keywords: two weeks, no verdict
  • Jetpack Compose splits Korean between syllables, but the stacked 'R/u/l/e' label came from how a Row measures

item.title: Claude Code on WSL vs native Windows: what changed – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Method

Claude Code on WSL vs native Windows: what changed after the move

Moving Claude Code from WSL to native Windows took one day for the repos and four more for session logs and Docker. The session logs need new folder names, a rewritten cwd and longer retention.

This is a checklist for anyone running Claude Code inside WSL (the Windows Subsystem for Linux) who wants to move to native Windows. We moved the repos and tools in one day, October 18, 2026, and verified them with an R8 release build and 1,500 monkey events. Session logs and Docker took until October 22.

In those four days the agent got five things wrong: session logs nearly disappeared, its advice for stopping WSL also stopped Docker, and plugins in daily use were removed. The eight steps below are ordered with those mistakes in mind.

The checklist, in eight steps

We had used WSL because Claude Code used to be slow in the Windows terminal, with many features not working. On October 18 the operator asked whether Windows was usable now; the agent said yes and suggested trying one project for a day or two first. The operator said to move everything at once, and when approving the tool installs, told it to run a build as well. Keeping the projects in WSL and opening them from Windows through the WSL network path was ruled out because the agent called that path very slow (we never timed it).

If you follow this order, most of what went wrong for us gets caught early.

  1. Copy projects from the WSL home to the Windows home. Don't move them. Leave out node_modules, build, .gradle, .dart_tool, .next and .cxx.
  2. Run git status --porcelain | wc -l in every repo on both sides and make sure the counts match.
  3. Set core.filemode=false (submodules too), switch repos with symlinks to core.symlinks=true and check the links out again, run git worktree repair, and fix sdk.dir in Android's local.properties.
  4. Check tool versions and install what's missing per user, without admin rights.
  5. Rewrite the environment section of your Claude Code instruction file and delete workarounds that only WSL needed.
  6. Raise cleanupPeriodDays before you copy session logs. Then copy them under the new folder names, rewrite cwd inside them, and look for logs in .claude/projects under the WSL root account's home too. Sessions that kept running in WSL after the move need one last sync. Finally, open claude --resume in each project folder and check the old sessions are listed; run it from any other folder and the session is saved under a separate project folder.
  7. Turn off whatever wakes Ubuntu, and if you run Docker Desktop, stop only Ubuntu with wsl --terminate <distro>. You're done when wsl -l -v shows Ubuntu as Stopped and docker-desktop as Running. If you change .wslconfig, applying it takes one wsl --shutdown, and Docker stops briefly with it (our containers were back within a minute).
  8. Install an R8 release build on an emulator, run 1,500 monkey events, and check the crash buffer and that the process is still alive.

These are the commands we used for steps 1 and 3, gathered into one block, with repo names replaced by placeholders. Links inside a repo were found as the files git records with mode 120000.

# step 1 (inside WSL)
rsync -a --no-links --exclude=node_modules --exclude=build --exclude=.dart_tool \
  --exclude=.gradle --exclude=.next --exclude=.cxx <folders> <Windows home>/
# step 3 (Git Bash, per repo)
r=<repo>
git -C "$r" config core.filemode false
git -C "$r" submodule foreach --quiet 'git config core.filemode false'
export MSYS=winsymlinks:nativestrict
git -C "$r" config core.symlinks true
git -C "$r" ls-files -s | awk '$1=="120000"{ $1=$2=$3=""; sub(/^ +/,""); print }' > "$TMP/links.txt"
while IFS= read -r p; do rm -f "${r:?}/${p:?}"; done < "$TMP/links.txt"
tr '\n' '\0' < "$TMP/links.txt" | xargs -0 git -C "$r" checkout --
git -C <main repo> worktree repair <worktree paths...>

Git settings for the copied repos

From inside WSL, rsync -a --no-links copied 35 folders (16 of them worktrees of our game repo) and one bundle file to the Windows home, about 1.5 GB once build outputs were excluded. The WSL originals stayed where they were as a backup. That was the operator's rule, and we went back to those originals twice to recover session logs the first pass had missed.

Because of --no-links, rsync skipped every symlink with "skipping non-regular file". In the three repos that had links, we set core.symlinks=true, exported MSYS=winsymlinks:nativestrict in Git Bash, deleted the placeholder files and ran git checkout on them. In the utilities repo, CLAUDE.md came back as a real link to AGENTS.md. Every repo and submodule got core.filemode=false so permission-bit differences don't show up as changes. The game repo's 16 worktrees still pointed at Linux paths in their .git files; git worktree repair fixed the "gitdir incorrect" entries.

To check the copy, we compared the git status --porcelain line count of each repo against the WSL original: 23 lines in one repo, 0 in another, and so on. All matched except one repo, where a browser download marker, …pptx:Zone.Identifier, had been committed by mistake. Windows doesn't allow a colon in file names, so the file couldn't be created; git update-index --skip-worktree told git to ignore it.

The trees copied this way stayed mostly LF. The fresh work trees our harness later checked out for each repository came out CRLF because of core.autocrlf=true, and checks that count bytes broke four times in a month. That record is in Claude Code on Windows: CRLF broke four checks.

Tool versions, and two workarounds we deleted

The WSL-era instruction file listed node 20 and python 3.10. Windows already had node 22 and python 3.12, so the environment section we rewrote that morning used those (v22.18.0 and 3.12.3 as of November 2). The java on PATH was a Java 8 JRE with no javac, so JDK 21 went into the user folder from a zip and Gradle was pointed at it with org.gradle.java.home in ~/.gradle/gradle.properties. The winget install of the Google Cloud CLI stalled on a UAC prompt that was never approved, so we unpacked Google's zip into the user folder and added it to the user PATH. In Git Bash it has to be called as gcloud.cmd. jq, which WSL never had, and rg, which Windows lacked, came from winget with --scope user.

Some of our Android projects live on another Windows drive. Under WSL that drive was mounted over the 9p file system, Gradle's lock files broke there, and the instruction file told the agent to pass a separate --project-cache-dir or build from a copy on the Linux side. On native Windows the drive is used directly, so the new file drops that rule. A second line went too: "flutter on PATH is the Windows SDK, so call the Linux SDK by absolute path" no longer applies with only the Windows SDK left. Across the 5 sessions for projects on that drive since the move (81 jsonl files counting subagent logs), Timeout waiting to lock and Could not lock appear zero times, though few full builds ran there in that period.

Session logs live outside the project folder

With every project copied, claude --resume on Windows still showed none of the old sessions. Claude Code keeps session logs under ~/.claude/projects/, in a folder named after the working directory's absolute path. A project folder in the Linux home maps to -home-<user>-<project>, and the same folder in the Windows home maps to C--Users-<user>-<project>. On the night of October 18 we copied the 14 folders that had logs (about 3.1 GB) under their new names.

They still didn't show up as of October 21, because every line in a log carries a "cwd" field, and those still held Linux paths. When the agent tried to rewrite them in bulk, Claude Code's automatic permission check blocked it as tampering with session transcripts. We didn't work around the check. The agent wrote a script that changes only cwd, the operator ran it with a ! command, and 31 files were rewritten.

In each log, the script changes the cwd value from the Linux path to the Windows path and leaves the conversation text and the file's modification time alone. It only rewrites the top-level session files; subagent logs in subfolders are left as they are. Sessions opened outside the home (on another drive, for example) need their own line for that path. Below is the actual script with the second-drive handling and the user name taken out, and the Windows home detected automatically. If you run it with ! from Git Bash, pass the script path with forward slashes; the shell strips backslashes, which is why our first run couldn't find the file.

# Rewrite only cwd in copied session logs (.jsonl) to Windows paths. Keeps mtime.
import os, re, glob
LINUX_HOME = '/home/<user>'
WIN_HOME = os.path.expanduser('~')          # %USERPROFILE%
root = os.path.join(WIN_HOME, '.claude', 'projects')
pat = re.compile(r'"cwd":"' + re.escape(LINUX_HOME) + r'((?:/[^"]*)?)"')
def rep(m):
    # inside a JSON string, so backslashes are doubled
    path = (WIN_HOME + m.group(1).replace('/', '\\')).replace('\\', '\\\\')
    return '"cwd":"%s"' % path
n = 0
for f in glob.glob(os.path.join(root, '*', '*.jsonl')):
    with open(f, encoding='utf-8') as fh:
        s = fh.read()
    if '"cwd":"' + LINUX_HOME not in s:
        continue
    st = os.stat(f)
    with open(f, 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='') as fh:
        fh.write(pat.sub(rep, s))
    os.utime(f, (st.st_atime, st.st_mtime))
    n += 1
print('rewritten', n)

That is when we noticed five logs from September 18 to 20 were gone. The agent had kept the original modification times when copying, and by default Claude Code deletes logs untouched for more than 30 days when it starts. We added "cleanupPeriodDays": 3650 to ~/.claude/settings.json and copied the five back from WSL.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Eight missed root logs, and a shutdown that took Docker down

On the night of October 22 the operator said the session logs didn't seem to have come across properly. The agent had already reported the job finished. A second look found it had missed all 8 logs under the WSL root account, and one session that kept running in WSL after the move was out of date. After those 9 were copied and their cwd rewritten, no log with a Linux path was left.

The agent was also wrong about stopping WSL. Six of its reports from October 18 to the afternoon of October 22 told the operator to ask for wsl --shutdown. On the night of October 22 the operator ran it, and Docker went down with it. Two more reports after that still carried the same line. --shutdown stops the whole WSL2 virtual machine, and Docker Desktop runs in a docker-desktop distro on that same VM. The command that stops only Ubuntu is wsl --terminate Ubuntu-22.04. When Ubuntu came back up afterwards, the likely cause was a find the agent had started inside Ubuntu earlier to search for session logs, still running.

Asked to remove one plugin, the agent read the request as all installed plugins and removed 22 user-scope plugins without looking at how often they were used. When the operator asked why things in use were being removed, the agent counted MCP calls in the last 60 days of session logs. The separately registered github and context7 MCP servers had 0 calls; among the removed plugins, Notion had 1,437 and playwright 59. Both went back in. Count calls before you remove a plugin.

Four things that kept waking Ubuntu

Keeping WSL as a cold backup only works if Ubuntu stays off. A script in the Startup folder that launched a bot inside WSL, the Ubuntu WSL integration in Docker Desktop's settings, a network drive permanently mapped into Ubuntu, and the leftover find above all started it. The script and the Docker settings were moved to a backup folder or switched off rather than deleted, and the drive was unmapped with net use and /delete. Our personal dashboard server on Docker had already been moved to a Windows path and a Docker volume, so it keeps running with Ubuntu stopped. The Ubuntu distro stays registered and Stopped as a backup; we're not deleting it.

The WSL2 VM that Docker Desktop uses stays up, so we shrank it in .wslconfig to memory=3GB, processors=2, swap=1GB and autoMemoryReclaim=dropCache. Opening the Linux entry in File Explorer, or any WSL network path, starts Ubuntu again; --terminate it when that happens.

Calling it done: an R8 build and 1,500 monkey events

The R8 crash in our release gate note never showed up in a debug build, so we judged the environment move the same way: assembleRelease with --no-daemon for the image compressor app in our utilities repo. The first attempt lost its result when the session ended. The rerun, logging to a file, went through 337 tasks (298 executed, 39 from cache), including minifyReleaseWithR8, in 5 min 50 s. It was the first build on Windows, with no configuration cache yet.

adb -s emulator-5554 install -r app-release.apk
adb -s emulator-5554 logcat -c
adb -s emulator-5554 shell monkey -p <package> --throttle 200 --pct-syskeys 0 -v 1500
adb -s emulator-5554 shell pidof <package>
adb -s emulator-5554 logcat -d -b crash

On a Pixel 8 Pro API 35 emulator, monkey printed "Events injected: 1500" and "Monkey finished", pidof returned a process ID, and the crash buffer was empty. Two real phones were plugged in, but we didn't install on them, since that could overwrite the Play build. This run used install -r, which replaces an existing install, and we didn't check whether the app data was fresh. Defects that only show up on a fresh install are covered in the VIBRATE permission and fresh-install monkey test.

Step 3 fails on machines that can't create symlinks

On a machine that can't create native symlinks, step 3's core.symlinks=true re-checkout won't work as written (this one could). We didn't copy the Linux Flutter and Android SDKs and use the Windows ones instead.

No build-time comparison yet; only the operator saw the /resume list

We haven't timed the same build on native Windows and WSL under the same conditions. The agent never opened the /resume list itself; the last check was the operator saying on October 22 that it seemed to work. We also haven't checked whether the emulator lab's shell scripts were rerun on native Windows. The moved sessions still mention the old Linux paths in their conversation text, so on resume the agent may first try those paths. The agent's advice in its report was to tell it the new path once when resuming; we haven't looked for a better fix.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Can Claude Code run on Windows without WSL?

On this machine it does, using PowerShell and Git Bash side by side, through an Android release build and emulator tests. To paste an image on Windows, use Alt+V instead of Ctrl+V.

Can I move Claude Code session history from WSL to Windows?

Yes, but copying the folder isn't enough. Rename the folders under ~/.claude/projects/ to match the Windows paths and rewrite the cwd values inside the logs; after that, the operator reported that /resume seemed to work. Raise cleanupPeriodDays first, or older logs can be deleted.

What is the difference between wsl --shutdown and wsl --terminate?

--shutdown stops the whole WSL2 VM, which also stops Docker Desktop running on it. --terminate <distro> stops just that distro.

Checked 2026-11-02. Three Claude Code session logs from the move, the memory file that records it, and the global instruction file before and after. Times are Korea Standard Time.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Capping Vertex AI test costs: a 2,500 KRW stop line missed a 2,956 KRW bill, so we changed the defaults
  • Claude Code agents told to build a No. 1 app
  • Commits without a Co-Authored-By trailer: the agent made 26 of the 29 we could check
  • Claude Code scheduled runs: state left behind
  • Android 16 KB page size: add the linker flag before you upgrade the NDK (NDK 27 and 29 tinted our photos blue)
  • Claude Code data analysis: a 130% payback was 76%

item.title: Claude Code auto-compaction: what 9 summaries kept – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

What survives Claude Code auto-compaction: the summary, recent files and the memory index

After an auto-compaction, Claude Code carries on with one summary, a few recently read files and the memory index. The reasons behind decisions fall out of the summary, so write them into a memory file when they are made.

Giving an agent rules and limits 3/5

When a conversation nears its context limit, Claude Code shrinks everything so far into one summary and keeps going: auto-compaction. A session that ran ads and promotion for two of our games for 13 days was compacted nine times. Every summary carried the user's messages and the task list; none carried why the ad budget had been set to 2,000 won instead of the value in our ad runbook. What filled that gap, it appears, was a stale line in the memory index, reloaded after every compaction.

Nine auto-compactions, one summary page each

The session log has nine messages that begin "This session is being continued from a previous conversation", and nine compact_boundary records. All nine have trigger "auto"; nobody typed /compact. Each boundary record stores token counts before and after, and what survived was 2.6% to 8.2% of what was there before. Three of the nine happened on October 17.

#Time (KST)Tokens beforeTokens afterSummary length (chars)Ad budget or status
1Oct 11 00:12284,45712,96812,021(before ads came up)
2Oct 12 22:30216,51914,58310,549yes
3Oct 17 10:07484,39415,34612,941yes ("all 4 paused")
4Oct 17 17:49533,37713,92113,364no
5Oct 17 22:12307,76712,4499,730yes
6Oct 18 21:59439,90216,19213,897yes
7Oct 19 12:02243,56114,94412,250yes
8Oct 19 22:35241,76014,81711,656no
9Oct 20 15:39202,85216,72011,008no

Every summary had the same sections, including "All user messages", "Pending Tasks", "Current Work" and "Optional Next Step". Ads first came up on October 11; of the eight summaries after that, five mention a budget amount or whether a campaign was on or off. The word "runbook" appears in none of the nine, and neither does the reason the campaigns were split by language (Korean creatives shown to non-Korean speakers waste impressions).

Two other things came back right after each compaction. Recently read files were re-attached, two to five each time. The ad memory file was among them only after compactions 3 and 5. The memory index came back too, as instructions on the next user turn: ten times in all, once at the start and once after each compaction. From October 19 on, the global CLAUDE.md came back with it four times.

For comparison we counted an app development session and a game development session. In both, the user ran /compact by hand five times. Those ten summaries ran 9,317 to 20,634 characters, all had the same four sections, and none of the ten commands had instructions after it.

To count the same things in your own sessions, run these three lines on a session log. Logs live under ~/.claude/projects/<working folder name>/, one jsonl per session.

grep -c '"subtype":"compact_boundary"' <session>.jsonl   # compactions
grep -c '"isCompactSummary":true' <session>.jsonl        # continuation summaries
grep -c '"type":"AutoMem"' <session>.jsonl               # times the memory index was loaded

This session gives 9, 9 and 10.

The 25,000 won budget came from a session with no compaction

Our first guess was that after a summary the agent fell back to the values in the runbook, our written ad procedure. The logs put that event on the night of October 8, with no compaction involved. At 21:56 the operator opened two Claude Code sessions at once, each driving Chrome to build a Google Ads app campaign: one for Arrow Knots, one for Block Turn. Neither session was ever compacted.

  • 21:57 The operator told the Arrow Knots session: 2,000 won a day, no target cost per install (CPI), all countries. In the same minute the Block Turn session read the runbook its brief pointed to.
  • 22:07 The Block Turn session asked whether to keep the runbook's target CPI of 1,400 won and daily budget of 25,000 won, since those were set for the US.
  • 22:11 The operator replied "analyze it properly and go ahead", with nothing about budget.
  • 22:14 The agent typed 25000 into the daily budget, and 700 won as the target CPI (not the runbook's 1,400 either).
  • 22:22 The operator repeated the instruction, sharply: 2,000 won a day, no CPI, all countries.
  • 22:23 The agent wrote a memory file.

The agent's mistake was at 22:14: it asked about the budget, got "go ahead", and read that as approval of the runbook value. The 2,000 won instruction had gone to the other session 17 minutes earlier, at 21:57, and two sessions do not share context. One level further back, both the runbook and the ad plan document said 25,000 won. The runbook was a plan to measure US install costs, spending a 100,000 won cap over four days, and the plan the game development session wrote at 19:19 that day said "25,000 won a day for 14 days". The operator's new decision was in no file at all.

That game development session's last manual compaction, at 00:47 on October 9, produced a summary that still said "ad plan: KR, 25,000 won/day", 2 hours 25 minutes after the Block Turn session had been corrected to 2,000 won at 22:22.

October 17: Arrow Knots KR called "running" while paused

At 08:08 on October 17 the marketing session's agent read the Ads console: Block Turn KR running at 4,000 won a day, Arrow Knots KR at 2,000 won, both English campaigns paused. At 08:41 it advised the operator to pause Arrow Knots KR or move its budget to Block Turn KR.

At 09:12 the agent edited that very ad memory file, adding only a note about account linking. The line from October 11, "all four ad groups run until Nov 2", stayed. What was still right in that file was the decision not to use the runbook values; its amounts (2,000 won each) and its status no longer matched the console that morning. The summary from compaction 3 at 10:07 said "all 4 game campaigns paused (by the user or the other session)"; the one from compaction 4 at 17:49 had no ad status at all.

None of the five files re-attached after compaction 4 was an ad memory file. At 19:24, on the next user turn, the memory index was reloaded, and its two ad lines read "English (Southeast Asia) / Korean, 2 campaigns, 2,000 won/day each, no tCPI (overrides the runbook)" and "2 campaigns per language (KR / SEA EN), 2,000 won each, no tCPI". The index had said the same since the session started.

Fourteen minutes later, at 19:38, the agent called Arrow Knots KR a running campaign in two work logs, then asked the operator whether to add new creatives to it, and got a yes. Only after opening the campaign, at 20:39, did the agent report that it had been wrong and the campaign was paused; in the same report it noted that Block Turn KR was running at 4,000 won while its own notes said 2,000. At 21:08 the operator set the record straight: only Block Turn KR was running, at 4,000 won, and Arrow Knots was off. The agent said it had fixed "my note that still said 2,000 won each", and it changed three places: the Block Turn memory file, the Arrow Knots memory file, and the two ad lines in the index. The Block Turn file got a dated status line:

Status as of 2026-10-17 (confirmed by the user): of the four campaigns, only Block Turn KR runs, at 4,000 won/day; the rest are paused. Do not resume a paused campaign without the user's decision.

The summary from compaction 5 at 22:12 included the status table and a note that the agent had wrongly said "running", and the index reloaded after it read "as of 10/17 only Block Turn KR runs at 4,000 won, the other 3 paused".

The log does not say what the agent based "running" on. It may have remembered the morning's console reading, but that observation had become "all 4 paused" in summary 3 and was gone from summary 4, while the index came back 14 minutes before the mistake with the same "2,000 won each" wording the agent later used about its own notes. We take the index as the likelier source.

13 of 14 memory files end with Why and How to apply

This memory is the folder Claude Code keeps per working folder, ~/.claude/projects/<working folder name>/memory/, with MEMORY.md as a one-line-per-file index. As of November 2 the home folder's memory holds 14 files and a 14-line index. Thirteen end with Why: and How to apply:; the one without is a reference note about a plugin account. The ad memory was first written at 22:23 on October 8 and edited five more times through October 18. Its gist, minus identifiers and the operator's tone:

Block Turn install campaigns: one per language, 2,000 won/day each, no target CPI
Do not use the runbook §2 values "US, tCPI 1,400 won, 25,000 won/day".
Why: the user gave this instruction more than once and the runbook was followed instead.
How to apply: when setting or changing this campaign, the user's instruction beats the runbook.

No summary held the reason for overriding the runbook, yet in 13 days the marketing session never tried to set 25,000 won or a 1,400 won target CPI. It had read this file on October 11 while drafting an ad plan, and the index line's "(overrides the runbook)" came back at the start and after compactions 1 to 4. The October 17 fix rewrote that line as a status line, so the last five reloads carried no such phrase.

Write the reason for a decision into a memory file the moment it is made; do not count on a summary to carry it. And for anything a person can change outside the conversation, like an ads console, trust neither the summary nor the memory.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The runbook, /compact instructions, CLAUDE.md, the index

One option is to change the runbook to 2,000 won. But its §2 numbers belong to a US cost experiment (100,000 won over four days), while what actually ran was a different experiment split by language, English in Southeast Asia and Korean in Korea. The §2 values were never changed, and the logs do not say why. The memory file says not to use them.

Picking compaction points by hand did not help either: the game development session's manual summary still carried the 25,000 won plan. A decision made in another session cannot reach a summary unless it enters this session as a message or a file. Relying on the summary's list of user messages fails for the same reason: the 2,000 won instruction was a message in the neighboring session, and the operator pausing a campaign in the console was not a message at all. Adding instructions after /compact about what to keep is something we have not tried; all ten manual compactions here ran without any.

The global CLAUDE.md was also reloaded with the index after compactions 6 to 9 (from October 19 on). Since it comes back the same way, we expect status written there to go stale the same way. What came back just before the October 17 mistake was an index line that mixed the decision with amounts, while the dated status line lived only in the file body. We recommend index lines that hold the decision and the file name, with amounts and on/off status kept, dated, in the file body.

A different working folder means a different memory

Claude Code kept memory per working folder. Sessions opened in the game repository's folder wrote to a separate memory folder, and its ad status file said "on 10-17 the user paused everything; Block Turn KR resumed the same day at 4,000 won".

If a session finishes without compaction and nothing else runs alongside it, you will rarely need any of this. A status line with a date and "confirmed by the user" is only right until the next change.

What to do when a decision departs from the docs

  1. When the operator gives a value that differs from a document, create one memory file on the spot: the decision, the document and value it overrides ("do not use"), Why:, then How to apply:.
  2. Put only that file's decision in the MEMORY.md index, as one line. Leave amounts and on/off status out of it.
  3. Keep current status, such as which campaigns are on, on a separate line in the file body with a date and "confirmed by the user", plus what must not change ("do not resume a paused campaign without the user").
  4. Put this in How to apply: "before any console action that spends money, read the current console values; if they differ from this file's status line, fix the file first." When Arrow Knots KR was turned back on on October 18, the memory and index were updated that same evening.

Our note Claude Code subagent prompts: rules after 5 cut-off agents records the same thing from the other side: agents cut off by usage limits, and the files they left on disk.

The runbook still says 25,000 won, and the index still holds status

On November 2 the runbook's §2 and the ad plan document still say 25,000 won. The index's Block Turn line on the same day still carries status ("as of 10/18 Block Turn KR 4,000 won and Arrow Knots KR 2,000 won running"), so by step 2 that line is the first one to cut back to the decision. The exact time Arrow Knots KR was paused is not in the session logs, so we could not measure it.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Giving an agent rules and limits: all 5 parts

  1. When Claude breaks a rule written in CLAUDE.md: six incidents and what came back
  2. A permission table for a scheduled AI agent: what it does alone, and which clicks a person makes

FAQ

What is left after Claude Code auto-compacts a session?

In this session, one summary of about 10,000 to 14,000 characters plus two to five recently read files. All nine summaries had sections for user messages, pending tasks, current work and next step, and the tokens after compaction were 2.6% to 8.2% of those before.

Does Claude Code memory survive compaction?

The index did. In this session MEMORY.md was loaded ten times, at the start and after each of the nine compactions. Memory file bodies came back only after compactions 3 and 5, as recently read files.

Does running /compact by hand give a more accurate summary?

These logs do not show that. Ten manual compactions without instructions produced summaries with the same four sections, and the game development session's summary still carried a 25,000 won plan that another session had already replaced.

Sources: five Claude Code session logs, the memory files and index, and the ad runbook and plan. Counts were redone from the logs on November 2, 2026; times are KST. Ad account identifiers are left out.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Capping Vertex AI test costs: a 2,500 KRW stop line missed a 2,956 KRW bill, so we changed the defaults
  • App privacy policy templates: we threw ours out and rewrote it from a code audit
